maintopic: ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE
ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE
subtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA-ANNOUNCEMENT RESPECTING EMIGRATION OF DOUKHOBORS

speakeroldname: Hon. E. D. Fulton (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE
subtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA-ANNOUNCEMENT RESPECTING EMIGRATION OF DOUKHOBORS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I desire to make a statement in connection with the Doukhobor situation in British Columbia.
The government of Canada has been following closely the developments in the Kootenay area of British Columbia where, for many years, acts of violence, damage to property and disorder have been occurring. These occurrences have recently spread to other parts of the interior of British Columbia. The dominion government has shared the concern felt by all, and especially the citizens of British Columbia, over this situation.
While maintaining the view that the constitutional responsibility for the maintenance of law and order continues to be that of the province, the government of Canada has felt that the most recent series of outbreaks, especially, have demanded a readiness on its part to give sympathetic consideration to co-operating with the province in any specific request or proposal put forward by the province which offers real possibility of a solution of the problem.
In accordance with this spirit, representatives of the dominion government have recently participated in extensive negotiations with representatives of the government of British Columbia in connection with a particular suggestion advanced by the latter as a solution to the problem. This involves the suggestion that members of the Doukhobor sect associated with the sons of freedom, who have for many years insisted that they are in conscience unable to accept and
abide by the laws of this country, be assisted in their expressed desire to emigrate to Russia.
In the course of these discussions, and in keeping with the attitude outlined above, the dominion government indicated to the province its willingness to accept a generous share of the burden of implementing this proposal. As a result of these discussions, the following joint statement has been agreed to by the two governments. The text is as follows:
This statement is made by the governments of Canada and British Columbia jointly in the belief that certain members of the Doukhobor sect associated with the sons of freedom earnestly desire to leave Canada forever and is made for the purpose of establishing the intention of the two governments to co-operate so that those persons may carry out their desire.
Those desiring to take advantage of this offer will be required to declare their intention on or before the 30th day of September, 1958, and arrangements will be made to complete migration as soon as possible after this date. Those desiring to leave Canada should at once communicate with the office of the dominion director of citizenship and immigration in Vancouver or with the government agent at Grand Forks, Rossland or Nelson in the province of British Columbia.
The governments of Canada and British Columbia are agreed that upon being advised by the U.S.S.R. that the Soviet union will accept applying Douk-hobors of that sect as immigrants into that country:
(1)	the governments will assist and co-operate with individuals, families and groups desiring to migrate, in the furnishing and securing of all necessary documents, visas and passports required for the purpose;
(2)	the government of British Columbia will assist in restoring to their parents custody of their children for whom parents make application for the purpose of emigration from Canada;
(3)	reasonable financial assistance will be provided (a) by the government of Canada to cover the cost of transportation to the U.S.S.R.; and (b) by the government of British Columbia to assist in the establishing of settlers in that country in an amount not to exceed transportation assistance and for a period subsequently to be determined;
but upon the condition that all such financial assistance will be made available only to persons renouncing Canadian citizenship;
(4)	the government of British Columbia will assist, if asked, in the orderly realization of assets real or personal of migrating persons and will credit moneys thereby secured as directed by them.
The government of Canada will co-operate in arranging for and facilitating discussions between representatives of the Doukhobors and of the Soviet government in Canada regarding the arrangements to be made for admission to Russia of those desiring to migrate.
Those who do not within the time specified accept this offer to assist in migrating from Canada will be understood to desire to remain in Canada subject
3580	HOUSE OF
Doukhobor sect-Proposed Emigration to all laws, municipal, provincial or federal, governing Canadian citizens and privileged as heretofore to enjoy the rights and liberties of such citizenship.
That is the end of the joint statement. I may say that the text of this joint statement is also released this morning in Victoria at this time by the government of British Columbia.

maintopic: ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE
subtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA-ANNOUNCEMENT RESPECTING EMIGRATION OF DOUKHOBORS
speechtext: I am sure the house will have listened with great interest to the statement of the minister on behalf of the federal government, and I can only say on behalf of the opposition that we hope this arrangement between the federal government and the government of British Columbia will work out satisfactorily and that these people will be able to find the tranquillity elsewhere which they apparently think they cannot find here in Canada.

maintopic: ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE
subtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA-ANNOUNCEMENT RESPECTING EMIGRATION OF DOUKHOBORS
speechtext:
As
the member representing the constituency which is the focal point of the problem with which the minister has dealt, may I say that without a doubt the house has listened with great interest to the minister's unprecedented and unusual statement concerning the agreement between the federal government and the government of British Columbia to deal with an unusual situation and in response to a most unusual request. We in this group trust that co-operation between the federal government and the government of British Columbia will result in a final solution to this long-standing and most difficult problem to the satisfaction of all parties concerned.
We are glad the government of Canada has extended its co-operation to the government of British Columbia, and I compliment the minister for his patience, constructive approach and deep concern and interest in this question. I do urge both governments to enlist the co-operation of the district consultative committee, which is composed of representative citizens who have a great understanding of the situation, circumstances and other aspects of this problem.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: AIRPORTS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Transport. In view of the fact that since the start of construction of the new Dorval airport terminal conditions have changed due to the jet era, will the minister consider the recommendation made by both the international civil aviation organization and the international air transport association to the effect that air conditioning will be a must in air terminals in the jet age, according to a report which appeared on August 13 last in the Montreal Star?

speakeroldname: Hon. George H. Hees (Minister of Transport):
maintopic: AIRPORTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for giving me notice of his intention to ask this question. When planning was under way in the 1954-55 period, air conditioning was considered but not included at that time since it has not been usual to include air conditioning in government buildings unless special reasons justify this. Air conditioning would have added about 10 per cent to the cost of the building, or about $1J million.
Requirements relating to jet aircraft use were not known in 1954 to either the air lines or the planners, and it was only last year that the international aviation experts decided that there was good reason at terminals where commercial jets are parked close at hand for sealing the building completely against the noise and, therefore, for air conditioning at Dorval. The jets will park 500 feet away at an aeroquay.
To introduce air conditioning at this stage would require material delays in completion of construction, something I do not favour in view of the great need for the building. However, because we have provided adequate duct space in the public waiting room area, limited air conditioning could be added at a later stage if experience should make this necessary and desirable.

speechtext:
At the close of last night's sitting, Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Laurier was directing some questions to me with respect to certain boards concerning the regulation of lake Ontario and the St. Lawrence river on which my department has representation. There was some confusion at the time as to which board the hon. member had reference. I think this statement will give the complete story.
At the present time the department, through the director of its water resources branch, has membership on two boards which were appointed by the international joint commission and which report to that body with respect to the regulation of the levels of lake Ontario and the St. Lawrence river.
With respect to the regulation of the levels of lake Ontario and the St. Lawrence river, the international lake Ontario board of engineers was appointed by the international joint commission in April of 1953 under terms of reference from the governments of Canada and the United States dated June 25, 1952. It is a two-man board upon which Canada has one member, an engineer of my department.
The international St. Lawrence river board of control was appointed by the international joint commission on November 16, 1953 under the terms of an order of approval of that body dated October 29, 1952 in connection with the application of the government of Canada to the international joint commission:
-far an order of approval for the construction of certain works for the development of power in the international rapids section of the St. Lawrence river.
[DOT]-dated June 30, 1952. This is a six-man board upon which Canada has three representatives, one of whom is an engineer of this department, who is also a member of the previously mentioned board and who is chairman of the Canadian section of the board of control.
The international lake Ontario board of
engineers submitted to the international

"death

joint commission on May 5, 1955 a plan of regulation, No. 12-A-9, to which the hon. member referred last evening. This plan was designed to protect the interests located upstream and downstream from the power works in accordance with the range of levels and criteria tentatively adopted by the commission in March, 1955.
At this meeting representations were made on behalf of the province of Quebec to obtain greater assurance that the adopted plan of regulation would provide the downstream interests with adequate protection. The commission directed that the board incorporate such minor adjustments as might be necessary to best meet these requirements. This direction resulted in the development of a plan known as plan No. 12-A-9CM). Although plan 12-A-9(M) had not been presented to the commission or to the governments formally, the governments took into consideration the results of this plan, particularly in regard to its similarity to plan 12-A-9 with respect to its critical profiles for channel excavations, and the adjustments it contained to satisfy downstream interests. Accordingly, in the government's reply of December 3, 1955 to the commission's letter of May 9, 1955, plan 12-A-9 was approved for the purpose of calculating critical profiles and the design of channel excavations only. The commission's recommended range of stage of 244, navigation season, to 248 as nearly as may be, and the recommended criteria for the operation of regulatory works were approved.
In so far as the work of the international lake Ontario board of engineers in developing a plan of regulation was concerned, the commission considered that it had completed its assignment and it directed that the board should complete a documentation of its regulation studies in a form in which the commission could present the material to the international St. Lawrence board of control, the body charged with responsibility for the operation of the plan, for the study of further refinements of that plan. The board of control undertook these further studies and in June, 1958 presented to the commission plan of regulation No. 1958-A, which plan was adopted by the commission at a meeting in Montreal on July 14 last.
The present status of the international St. Lawrence board of engineers is that it is completing its studies with respect to factors affecting the levels of lake Ontario as requested in the terms of reference of June 25, 1952.
The international St. Lawrence river board of control is continuing its co-operation with the joint board of engineers, a body appointed
Supply-Northern Affairs by the governments of Canada and the United States to act for them in ensuring adequate construction programs, plans and specifications. With the completion of construction the board of control will assume the responsibility of carrying out all provisions of the orders of approval of October 29, 1952 and July 2, 1956 related to the water levels and regulations of discharge of water from lake Ontario.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: The minister went on to deal with a still further amendment adopted on July 14, 1958 in Montreal, known as plan 1958-A. Has that plan received the approval of the international joint commission by way of amendment to the original order of approval?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: It has been approved by the international joint commission, but the order of approval has not been amended.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I know that much of this is technical and I will not unduly pursue the matter. Perhaps I can wind up my remarks by this question. Returning to the board of control, the minister gave to the house a moment ago an outline of the duties and responsibilities of that board. Having regard to the present levels arising out of the development of power in the international section, those levels are to be held at 238 for the first ten years. I have been informed that there is a possibility that this will be changed and that the levels will not be held at 238 for that period but might well be increased to 242 before the end of the ten years. Is that matter under study by the board of control, and have they made any recommendation in that respect?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I am informed that this matter is not under study by the

Supply-Northern Affairs international board of control, and that no specific proposition has been made by that board.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: It may not be under study, but one of their duties is to supervise for a period of ten years the operation of the levels, and may I have an answer from the minister or his advisers as to whether or not there is any change in the original idea of allowing the level to remain at 238 for ten years?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I am informed that any change such as that suggested would have to come as a direction from the international joint commission.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Then going back to plan 12-A-9(M) and plan 1958-A, which I take it have been considered by the minister's officers in order to protect the downstream interests-that is to say, in order to protect the development of power at Beauharnois -so that nothing which is done upstream will in any way affect the power development at Beauharnois and so that nothing which is done upstream will affect the level in the port of Montreal, is the minister satisfied that these two plans will adequately protect the safety of the interests in these two areas?
In so far as this can be done, will it protect both these interests; first, power development at Beauharnois and second, the level of the water in the port of Montreal?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I think everyone in the constituencies around the great lakes is interested in this Illinois development which, I understand, a senate committee has approved, and it is quite likely that this diversion will go ahead, at least for a certain period of time. The Canadian Department of External Affairs sent an aide memoire in relation to this subject indicating that the Canadian position is that while Canadians are not in favour of this diversion it is completely within the right of the United States to go ahead with it.
I want to ask whether the Canadian Department of External Affairs received any advice from the water resources branch with regard to this; and second, if the diversion goes through, whether any studies are planned concerning any possible step that Canada might take, especially with regard to the lake Superior watershed, to compensate for the tremendous gallonage that is going to be taken out at Chicago.
[Mr. Hamilton (Qu'Appelle).)

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: The department of northern affairs, through its water resources division, did advise the Department of External Affairs about the effects of the Chicago diversion. There is, Mr. Chairman, as you know a present diversion to the great lakes watershed from Longlac which more than compensates for the water taken by the Chicago diversion. As far as I know there is no plan for any further diversion from the great lakes watershed into the great lakes system.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I may be dealing in fantasy, but I understand there has been a diversion from Lac St. Joseph westward in order to help the power set-up along the Manitoba border, and that there has also been a diversion of water which would originally have gone into the Hudson bay-James bay area, and I am just wondering whether there is any prospect of a more thorough study of the situation to determine whether we can afford to take still more water from the Hudson bay watershed and divert it into the lake Superior watershed or the Winnipeg river area?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: As a matter of fact the St. Joseph diversion is from the Hudson bay watershed into the lake Winnipeg or Nelson river watershed, and it does not affect the great lakes watershed. As to the question of diverting more water from the Hudson bay system into the great lakes system, I think that is purely a matter for the province of Ontario.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: May I ask the minister whether he is satisfied that this proposed diversion via Chicago, concerning which an aide memoire has been sent to the United States government, will not prejudicially affect Canadian interests in so far as upper lake levels are concerned?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: The facts are that such a diversion will prejudice the levels of the great lakes system and will reduce the power potential of that system.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: That is the point where I wondered about the study. There is more water up in that watershed, especially lying northeast of lake Nipigon, and I was just wondering whether the minister could not have some study conducted into ways and means of compensating for any diversion which might take place in the future. Even if the department does not go ahead with a concrete plan, would such a study not be worth while; or would the department already have the information necessary to know whether we could compensate for water taken out?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I think two
things should be cleared up. First of all, the proposed diversion has not gone through. As the Leader of the Opposition has said, we have made our view clear to the United States that taking more water would prejudicially affect both water levels and power production. As to the second point, dealing with the possible diversion of water from the Hudson bay watershed into the great lakes watershed, information is to some extent available but the view at the moment is that the possibilities would be limited by the economic factor, the cost.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
In view of the minister's
answer, may I ask whether the United States is entitled under international agreements to make this diversion which prejudices our interests, and if not, how does that country justify the action which it is proposing to take?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Yes, the United States is entitled to make the diversion, but there are certain factors prejudicial to both countries which we have been pointing out in the hope that they may see the weight of our arguments.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
I want to say a few words because of the importance of this vote in connection with the diversion of the Columbia river watershed in Canada and because of the great interest taken in this most important question by the people whom I have the honour to represent.
I notice that the vote is $227,780 this year as compared with $245,437 last year, a reduction of $17,657, which I presume indicates that the endeavour to obtain information is coming to an end. This is very different from the estimates we have had in previous years in connection with these studies.
I wish to express my appreciation of the good work which has been done by the staff of this branch of the minister's department, because it is their work which has made it possible to assess this situation in Canada. I also wish to express our appreciation-and when I say "our" I am speaking for the great majority of my constituents-of the good work done by the international commission and particularly by General McNaughton, who is highly regarded in my constituency. Most of my constituents believe that his foresight, patience and firmness in years past have contributed in great measure to the
Supply-Northern Affairs respecting of Canada's right to the development of her own water works on the Columbia, and I think his position is now understood and appreciated to a much greater extent than it was a few years ago-to such a degree, indeed, that his arguments are now recognized as valid in the United States. And for the same reason that the United States authorities have the right to divert the waters which the Leader of the Opposition mentioned a few minutes ago, Canada has the right to divert the waters of the Columbia if Canada sees fit to do so.
I am one who hopes the government will be able to make an early arrangement which will be applied to all parties concerned for the commencement of the main dam on the Columbia river, wherever it may be located.
I understand there is a possibility of shifting it a short distance upstream or downstream from the earlier projected Mica creek location. However, I have two questions to ask the minister.
Can the minister inform the committee what this money will be spent on? Are the surveys entirely completed? Will this money be spent just on details of the report and so on? I understand the report of the engineering board on the Columbia development is expected some time late this fall. I am sure that is the basic document upon which this government will formulate its plans and its policies.
My second question is this. I do not expect the minister to be a prophet or to venture into the unknown and unseen, but because of the great interest in this question could he tell the committee in general terms what steps the government proposes to take after it has studied the report of the engineering board and has the facts before it to further the development of the hydro resources of the Columbia in Canada?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, perhaps before the minister replies I might make my observations on the same subject and he can deal with both of us at once. Before doing so may I join in the appreciation which has just been expressed for the work of the minister's officials in connection with this survey, which work has been as efficient as that of his officials in other branches of the department. I cannot give them any greater praise than that.
Perhaps the minister would indicate to the committee the progress which has been made in the survey in question, and perhaps also he would tell the committee whether pending the completion of this survey there have been any talks between the two governments on the diplomatic level to clear up some of the international legal principles involved, if

Supply-Northern Affairs they need clearing up, and which perhaps could be done while the survey is going on, thereby saving time.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to thank the hon. member tor Kootenay West for his gracious words to a great Canadian. In answer to his question concerning what steps will be taken after the report is submitted to the government, I believe the obvious conclusion would be that it will be studied. I believe I have already indicated to the committee that an economic study is under way now, the report of which is just about ready for presentation to the government, as I understand it. With the new engineering study to review the findings of previous engineering studies and the economic study to which I have referred, it is a matter of the government making a decision on what is the best means of proceeding from that point.
In reply to the question asked by the Leader of the Opposition concerning what talks have taken place with respect to the legal principles at stake, the answer is that discussions have been taking place but there has not been an exchange of views on global positions. Rather, there occurred an exchange of general views on the positions of the two governments.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, are these talks being held on the diplomatic level between representatives of the two governments or between officials of the minister's department and officials of the department concerned in Washington?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: This department does not carry out those discussions, but there have been discussions on the diplomatic level.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, these investigations were authorized by an order in council, No. 655, dated May 5, 1955. In general they are to determine what developments for the control of the water and incidental resources of the Fraser river basin in the judgment of the board would be advisable, practical and in the public interest, with particular reference to flood control and hydroelectric power generation.
The terms of reference contain such items as the following. There is reference to the fact that Canada and British Columbia shall share equally the cost of the said survey and report and the board shall render a preliminary report of its findings not later than June 30, 1958. I understand this has been received. It also provides that the board shall be terminated within a period of three months from the submission of the preliminary report unless the two governments agree that the board continue until the submission of the final report. maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not know if the minister is aware of the investigations that have been going on for the past several years at the University of British Columbia. There is a pilot project there largely financed by donations from private corporations to the university. Is this board acting in connection with that investigation? Is this one and the

same investigation, or are two investigations going on simultaneously, each doing basically the same work?

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES

Mr. Chairman, this investigation is concerned not only with the problem of fish versus power, but the pilot project in particular also deals with the problem of flood control. I regret that there should be an expenditure of public moneys for two investigations that are really doing very much the same work.
I know in more recent years the university investigation has paid a lot of attention to fish versus power. However, the initial project was concerned primarily with finding ways and means of controlling the waters of this river, and it was for this purpose that a large model of the Fraser river was constructed. If the Minister of Public Works would like to help us out so that we might have the record ironed out I have no objection.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: I understand, Mr. Chairman, it is not in this department, and I cannot give any more authentic information than I have given.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NORTHERN AFFAIRS AND NATIONAL RESOURCES
speechtext: Has the Fraser river board any offices out in British Columbia out of which their engineers conduct their operations? If so, would the minister be kind enough to advise where they are?

city of British Columbia is Victoria. Since they have their offices there they can utilize the provincial staffs and information which is collected there.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP LABOUR
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in rising to deal with the estimates of the Department of Labour and the unemployment insurance commission, I should first of all like to express my appreciation to the chairman and members of the committee on industrial relations. This committee has already considered these estimates and I would say, Mr. Chairman, that they have made some helpful and useful suggestions. However, on these estimates of the Department of Labour and the unemployment insurance commission I am sure members of this house in committee will have other questions to ask, and I shall try to be as helpful as I can in supplying the answers, with the advice and co-operation of my officials.
The total of these estimates, including the Department of Labour and the unemployment insurance commission, comes to $84,891,842, of which $71,359,500 relates to the unemployment insurance commission and $13,532,342 to the Department of Labour. The estimates of the Department of Labour exceed those of last year by $2,086,210, and those of the unemployment insurance commission are greater by $199,301 than last year.
Supplementary estimates totalling $1,547,435 are also being requested, bringing the total requirement to $86,439,277, an increase of $3,832,946 over last year for both departments. Of this amount, some $2 million is required to provide for expanded vocational training agreements with the provinces. There is also an increase of approximately $1 million in the government's contribution to the unemployment insurance fund.
Owing to greatly expanded activities, there is an increase of $676,000 in administration costs of the unemployment insurance commission. Hon. members will recall that an effort is being made to emphasize job-finding activities of the commission. This effort will be continued and augmented.

I should like briefly to touch on some of the programs in my department which are included in the estimates now before the house. In the field of industrial relations we are facing a situation where a number of one-year and two-year labour agreements have lately terminated or will terminate in the next few months. As a result of this fact, conciliation proceedings are under way in a number of different fields of industry.
I might mention at this time that during the year a total of 117 disputes in industries under federal jurisdiction were dealt with by the officers of my department. Of these, 53 were settled by these officers and 22 by conciliation boards. The others were in various stages of conciliation as the year ended.
Coming to the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act, may I say that I have given notice of my readiness to consider amendments to this act and that a number of suggestions have been received and are being considered at the moment.
I am still waiting for three major national organizations which have been requested to submit their recommendations, but to date I have not received them. However, on checking into the matter I find that they are in the process of completing their recommendations, and that they should be within my hands within the next few weeks.
Another matter which has been of major concern to my department has been the elimination of discrimination, whether it is based on race, religion or colour, throughout the labour field. It is my intention to set up a consultative committee representing interested groups to advise upon the administration of the fair employment practices act as it relates to discriminatory practices in industry.
One of the most important programs of the department is that concerning the rehabilitation of persons disabled or inhibited in one way or another from following their normal pursuits and earning a living for themselves and their families. It is encouraging to note that in this connection we have particulars of 1,055 persons who have been returned to useful employment during the last fiscal year. Previously the majority of these people were supported by public assistance, though this figure does not, of course, include all those who were to a greater or lesser degree assisted under this program.
In the civilian rehabilitation branch, in order to carry on the services rendered we are making provision for two additional employees to assist in the placement of older workers. This has been an aspect of labour problems in which I have been very interested for quite a number of years. Because of the
Supply-Labour
practice of certain industries of specifying certain ages, they have thereby eliminated many useful persons from employment. We are concentrating on this aspect of the matter by endeavouring to institute an educational program for employers, and by pointing out to them that the ability of a person is in no way diminished as the result of age but that in some respects the workmanship of an older person offers a great deal to a prospective employer.
As hon. members are well aware, my department carries on an extensive public information program relating to winter employment, and we have included in these estimates an amount of $150,000 for the continuation this year of this program. I might mention that in pursuance of this objective of alleviating and improving the winter employment situation I called a conference in Ottawa. This conference was attended by representatives of provincial labour departments, national organizations and others interested in finding a solution to this pressing problem. The recommendations of the conference are now being studied by my department and will shortly be submitted to the government for active consideration.
I think I can say however, that the conference did serve to heighten the realization of the extent of this problem and to place the problem squarely before a number of persons and groups in a position to take concerted action in order to deal with it. As a result of the conference I think there is a greater awareness of the whole situation, and that there will be the maximum degree of co-operation from provincial labour departments, labour and management group!! and other interested bodies in order to evolve measures by which to deal with the situation.
Another matter with which my department is concerned is vocational training, and new agreements have been reached with the provinces which call for further federal expenditure in this field. I do not think I need to emphasize in this house the importance of programs to provide increased facilities for trade and technological training in this country. Hon. members are aware, as I am aware, of the need for adding to the pool of trained and skilled labour in Canada, and I do not think I go too far in describing this objective as a national necessity.
In respect of this field of vocational training I should like to bring to the attention of this house the fact that the existing agreements will make available a total of $40 million from the federal government to the provinces over the next five-year period. Of this amount $25 million will be allotted for buildings and

Supply-Labour
equipment and $15 million for operational expenses on a matching basis.
The Department of Labour is also continuing to study the effects upon industry of recent technological changes including automation, and I feel the results of these studies will have a useful application in determining the effects of such changes on manpower and training needs for the future.
Returning now to the unemployment insurance commission, I would like to point out that there were several extensions of seasonal benefits last year and this year, and that discriminatory regulations against married women were removed. Fishermen were brought under this act, and added administrative requirements in connection with these changes account in part for the increased costs relating to this department. In connection with the unemployment insurance fund, I tabled a report on July 10 which gives the current state of the fund, and the table relating to the fund can be found on page 2137 of Hansard for that date.
In order to emphasize the job-finding function of the national employment service I am asking this year for 150 new positions for placement personnel, and provision for this will be found in the supplementary estimates of the unemployment insurance commission. The purpose of this additional staff is of course so they will be able this winter to activate the job-finding program of the national employment service, which will mean that we will not be content merely to pay benefits but that a positive and energetic effort will be made to place people who are without jobs.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP LABOUR
speechtext:
The committee will have listened with interest to the statement the minister has just made on the first item of his estimates, which gave him an opportunity to discuss generally the work and the problems of his department. I think the committee will have been struck by the fact that although he spoke on a good many matters-not, of course, in detail-he did not deal at this time with what I consider to be the most pressing matter from his point of view and that of his department, namely the problem of employment and unemployment. Perhaps he intends to do this later after he has heard from us.
The minister mentioned the desirability of removing all discrimination and the further steps he is taking to ensure that this will be done. I am sure he will get general support from this house in the achievement of that most important and desirable objective. He also mentioned the work of his department in respect to rehabilitation of and work for the handicapped, which is also important and

must commend all our support and sympathy. He also mentioned the problems of the older workers, which make an appeal to our sympathy, especially those of us who will soon be joining the ranks of the older workers. Then he just touched upon one of the most important of all labour problems, which is very much in the minds of labour at the present time in view of technological developments in our industrial society, the problem of automation. We in this party have already given an indication of our realization of the importance of this problem by certain concrete suggestions we have made as to the responsibility of government in meeting it. It is certainly something which will have to increasingly engage the attention of the Minister of Labour and the Department of Labour.
The minister also mentioned-he did not do much more than mention-one of the most basic problems of all, a problem very much in our minds at the present time, that of industrial relationships. He called attention to the fact that this problem is looming up at the present time in certain specific respects in the form of the renegotiating of contracts between employers and employees in some of the most important industries in this country. There is no doubt that problems in this field, dangers in this field, are looming up, and if these problems are not solved and these dangers are not averted they will certainly add to our economic difficulties at a time when we already have enough economic difficulties. As the Prime Minister has said, and as I think the Minister of Labour has also said, the solution of this problem of industrial relationships at this time will require a sense of responsibility and restraint, and the exercise of this responsibility and restraint on the part of all concerned.
It seems to me that the basic problem of labour relations is more and more becoming one of the confrontation of huge corporate structures representing a concentration of great power-power not always controlled entirely in Canada-by huge union structures representing also a concentration of great power also not always controlled entirely in Canada. In this situation, which is very different indeed from the unbalanced one of say 50 years ago, then so heavily weighted against labour, both sides must recognize that new circumstances have developed and a new situation has arisen because of the growth of our industrial structure and the concentration of industrial economic and financial power into fewer and fewer hands.
As long as this is the case, and it is
inevitable that corporations should develop
in this way, surely both sides must recognize

that this has created new problems. It emphasizes in our minds not only the necessity for conciliation and solution but also the priority of the public interest. Governments .-in some cases in this field provincial governments, and in other cases the federal government-are the guardians of the public interest. In the discharge of that guardianship, that responsibility, governments I think have a duty to emphasize the necessity for social control, in certain circumstances, as a recognition of that public interest. Certainly, as I am sure the minister himself is very much aware, this situation has thrown new responsibilities on government as well as on workers and employers. Perhaps it necessitates a new approach to labour problems by government, one that will certainly preserve the rights of both sides, but subject always to the public interest.
I was glad to hear, and I am sure the committee was glad to hear, that recognition has been given to the seriousness of this problem; recognition of the desirability, perhaps, of a new approach to the problem of industrial relationships by the Department of Labour, and that ideas have been asked for by the department which would help them in the changes that may be required in the industrial relations act. Undoubtedly in view of this changing situation some changes are required to expedite and make more effective conciliation procedures, so that we may not be increasingly confronted with emergencies when those procedures have broken down, with the government having to step in and intervene by methods, at times, which no government desires to use or to be put into the position of having to use.
One could talk on this subject for a long time, and I have no doubt that some of my colleagues in my own party as well as members of the other opposition party will be discussing this aspect of the question. In the course of the remainder of my remarks, which will not be extensive, I propose to concentrate on unemployment. I hope to discuss the present situation in a way which may assist in steps which, perhaps, the Department of Labour can take toward meeting it. In view of the fact that I am now beginning a new subject, may I call it one o'clock?
At one o'clock the committee took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at 2.30 p.m.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OP LABOUR
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, at the luncheon recess I had reached the point of discussing a matter which, of course, is of primary
Supply-Labour
importance to the country and of equal importance I know to the minister and the Department of Labour, perhaps our most serious domestic problem, that of unemployment. As a matter which so directly concerns the Department of Labour and these estimates, I propose to deal with the present position as I see it, to discuss it frankly, but neither to make statements which I believe are not accurate or distort those I do make.
It is quite true that in recent weeks our economy in the face of deflationary pressures has shown a strength and resilience in some sectors which must be encouraging to all Canadians. It has also, of course, shown weaknesses, and those weaknesses are perhaps best illustrated by the employment picture in this country at this time. The situation I admit, and I have always admitted, is difficult and confused and in some respects almost contradictory. We have before us, and it is being emphasized more and more when discussions related to it take place in the house, a real and perhaps even a growing danger of inflation. The latest indication of the importance of that danger to the south of us-and whatever happens down there in these matters certainly affects us-is that today the federal reserve system in the United States has increased its discount rate through the federal reserve bank in San Francisco-and that will be followed I am sure by other banks-from If per cent to 2 per cent. The continuing danger of recession in the midst of this inflationary danger is shown, as I said, by the unemployment figures.
The two dangers, then, face us at the same time. I know, as other hon. members know, that this has certainly made it difficult for a layman to understand what is going on and what should be done to meet it. It has also confused the experts and the economists. We should, in fact we must face up to both these trends and try to analyse them in the hope that by a sober and intelligent analysis we can do something about them. However, parliament or the government cannot do anything about this problem if the existence of the problem and the dangers inherent in it are not recognized.
In attempting to assist in that recognition by producing facts which bear on it, we on this side of the house are continually charged with being promoters of doom and gloom and of shedding crocodile tears. Well, Mr. Chairman, this does not worry us, and it is not going to deter us from doing our duty as an opposition as we see it. But because these charges are continually levelled at us when we talk about the employment picture it makes it necessary for us to continue to

Supply-Labour
expose the insincerity of those charges by recalling the attitude of hon. members of the present government when they were sitting on this side.
I recall that at a time when winter unemployment in this country was under 200,000 the present Minister of Public Works moved and the present Prime Minister seconded a resolution which demanded the immediate appointment of a select committee to examine and do something about the unemployment situation which, in the words of the present Prime Minister as found at page 2099 of Hansard of February 15, 1954, was comparable to that of the beginning of the great depression. If hon. members will refer to page 2085 of Hansard of February 15, 1954, they will find a record of the discussion relative to the resolution to which I have referred.
During the 1955 session the opposition of that day demanded that a dominion-provincial conference on unemployment be called. My hon. friends may recall that they demanded it in very strong terms, and vigorously condemned the government of the day for not calling it. They made this demand at a time when the unemployment problem was less than half as serious as it is in 1958, and when it was a problem which this country pretty quickly solved.
Furthermore we should not forget that in those debates on unemployment in previous sessions the opposition of that day never failed to use the higher national employment service figures to support and at times exaggerate their claims. My hon. friend the Minister of Labour used to use those figures regularly, but I suppose when he talks on this matter later in this debate he will probably use the lower figures published by the dominion bureau of statistics.
When I have talked about unemployment inside and outside the house I have always used the dominion bureau of statistics figures, and when I have used the national employment service figures it has never been by themselves. There are two sets of figures, and perhaps neither gives the exact picture of what is happening. One set may exaggerate in one direction and one set in the other, but if the figures we have before us now, from whatever source they may come, turn out to be exaggerated and the dangers which are inherent in those figures turn out to be dangers which will be met and removed, then everyone in this committee and in the country will rejoice at that development. Meanwhile it is our duty to warn the government of the possibility of these dangers and try to convince it that something effective must be done to meet them through wise government policies.

I suggest it cannot be denied by any unprejudiced observer that we have been going through the worst period of unemployment since the depression of the thirties. Hon. members of the government I know will surely admit that now, even if they did not admit it in the debates in this house during last session. The members on the treasury benches have certainly changed their attitude on this question, because in the autumn session last year they did not give this house any indication that they appreciated the dangers of mounting unemployment. When they had to admit an abnormal situation had developed they tried either to minimize the seriousness of our economic troubles or else they claimed that unemployment was decreasing.
It is very interesting also to quote in this connection what various ministers had to say about this issue during the election campaign. As we are discussing the estimates of the Department of Labour perhaps I should limit myself in this regard to three statements made by the Minister of Labour. On February 20 he is reported as having said in Woodstock, Ontario, on February 19, the day before, and I quote from the Ottawa Journal of February 20:
"We believe unemployment is our responsibility and as long as one Canadian is unemployed we intend to do something about it."
We also attacked the former government's "tight money" policy as contributing to unemployment.
That is a remark which inspires certain ironic reflections in the light of what has happened in the last month or two. Then he said:
We gradually eased the tight money policy, dropping interest rates.
No doubt that was in the interests of creating employment. Well those interest rates have been increased by the present government since that statement was made. Then the Montreal Gazette of March 20 quotes the minister as saying:
Federal labour minister Michael Starr predicted last night the present unemployment situation will end by mid-June.
I shall have something to say about that in a moment, based on the official statistics on the subject. Then on March 28 the minister is reported by the Toronto Daily Star as having said:
Mr. Starr said that both he and the Conservative party had "great confidence in the future" and predicted that through various campaigns to be instigated this coming year, the problem of seasonal unemployment would be eliminated.
I hope the minister is right, but I suspect he will find it a little difficult to eliminate the problem of seasonal unemployment. While the Minister of Labour was saying during the

election campaign that unemployment would have disappeared by mid-June, the Minister of Finance in his budget speech, parts of which we have heard twice in this house, said as quoted on page 1233 of Hansard:
Once again the latest figures are encouraging, showing a rapidly narrowing gap in the percentage of unemployed as compared with a year ago.
I suggest, Mr. Chairman, with all respect to the Minister of Finance, that that is a misleading statement in the light of the official statistics on this subject. To support what I have just said we should look at the current situation as described by those official statistics, in order to see if those optimistic
Supply-Labour statements made by ministers are justified. For the purpose of the comparison I would like to make, I intend using the dominion bureau of statistics figures which certainly do not exaggerate, to say the least, the unemployment problem. In order to prove the points I want to make I should like at this stage to ask permission to insert a series of official statistics from the bureau of statistics, Canadian Statistical Review, which show for the first six months of 1957 and 1958, the number of persons in Canada having jobs, the number of unemployed and seeking work and the percentage of the total labour force unemployed. The statistics follow:
