These are official figures, Mr. Chairman, from the publications of the bureau about which I should like to make some observations. To begin with, let us look at the employment side. It can be seen from these figures from the bureau of statistics that the level of employment, not unemployment, has been lower in 1958 than it was in 1957 for all the months covered from January to June, except April. In January, 1958, there were
22.000	fewer people with jobs than in January, 1957. That figure was 48,000 in February and
56.000	in March. In April the trend was reversed and there were 11,000 more people with jobs than in April, 1957; but again in May, 1958-and this is significant-the figure was lower than in May, 1957, by 22,000, and in June it was lower by 40,000.
These figures, I think, lead to two conclusions. First, on the average for the first six months of this year, total employment has been lower than in 1957. This certainly must 57071-3-228
emphasize that we are in an abnormal situation, especially as you have to relate these employment figures to the increase in the labour force and the natural increase in population and the increase last year by immigration. With all that, our employment figures on the average for the six months of 1958 are lower. Second, since the month of April the employment gap, expressed in absolute terms as between 1958 and 1957, has been increasing. This means, I suggest, that the optimistic statements made by the Minister of Labour and the Minister of Finance are not supported by the facts and by the most recent information available to us.
Let us look at the unemployment situation, Mr. Chairman. Of course the number of unemployed, according to dominion bureau of statistics figures, has been decreasing steadily since March, 1958. That was to be expected with the seasonal pick-up, and we can all take satisfaction from that decrease. But perhaps it is more significant to consider

Supply-Labour
the gap in the percentage of unemployed this year as compared with last year. That gap is measured by dividing the percentage of the total labour force unemployed in 1958 by the same figure for each month in 1957.
If you apply that simple arithmetic you find that in January, 1958, the percentage of unemployed was 66 per cent higher than the year before; in February, 66 per cent; in March, 65 per cent; in April, 62 per cent. The figure went down a bit in April. In May it was 85 per cent higher and in June 92 per cent higher, and June is the last month for which figures are available. One cannot get very much comfort out of these facts. In other words, since April, 1958 the gap in the percentage of unemployed as compared with a year ago has been rising, and it has been rising significantly.
Now, surely this most important fact-and it is an important fact, and I am quite sure it worries the minister as much as it worries us-is in direct contradiction of what the Minister of Finance said in his budget speech at page 1233 of Hansard, which I have already mentioned and which was repeated in this house at page 3103 of Hansard as recently as August 5, when he quoted the unemployment figures for the month of June. On that last occasion in August he said, without, in my view, any regard for the facts:
These figures indicating the decrease in unemployment are, I think, figures that fully bear out what I had to say in the budget speech when I said, as found on page 1233: "Once again the latest figures are encouraging, showing a rapidly narrowing gap in the percentage of unemployed as compared with a year ago."
The figures I have quoted, Mr. Chairman- and they are official figures-show that the gap is not narrowing; it is widening.
My observations up to now have been limited to the unemployment situation as it has developed over recent months, and have been based exclusively on the most conservative figures published by the dominion bureau of statistics. I suggest that these statistics emphasize that the situation is still serious and I hope I will not be accused of presenting a gloomy picture merely because I put these figures on the record.
Now, what can we expect in this regard for the rest of the year and the beginning of 1959? Well, Mr. Chairman, I am not going to make any forecast about the unemployment situation in the immediate future. The responsibility for doing that and for giving the unemployment outlook to the house is, of course, that of the minister. Perhaps he will give us as clear and frank a statement as he can on this very important matter and on the policies the government intends to

initiate in order to cope with what I believe to be a continuing and serious situation.
Before the minister makes that statement I should like to give him some indications that might be of assistance to him in his presentation. In the first place I want to point out that according to our usual seasonal pattern in Canada-and this is, of course, to be expected-unemployment reaches its lowest levels in June, July, August and September. That has been the pattern over many years. But then it starts to rise again, even in periods of boom and prosperity, until the following April. In 1957, for instance, the percentage of the total labour force unemployed reached 2.7 per cent in June and remained at about that level for the following three or four months until it climbed to nearly 10 per cent, under the D.B.S. figures, in March, 1958. When the minister presents his employment outlook he will no doubt take into account the fact that in June of this year the percentage of unemployed was 5.2 and not 2.7 as it was last year.
In the second place, I am wondering whether or not the minister has studied the situation in the light of the conclusions of the famous hidden report, the "Canadian Economic Outlook for 1958". If he has he should then be in a position to answer some of the questions raised in excerpts from this report which have appeared and which have a very important bearing on the labour and employment situation in the country. One excerpt from the report reads:
In view of the downward momentum now present in the economy it is questionable whether any firming trend in the latter part of the year would be sufficient to bring over-all production for 1958 as a whole up to the level of the preceding year.
Meanwhile, available manpower, plant and other productive facilities will continue to increase. This means considerable slack is likely to persist in the economy throughout 1958 with unemployment remaining well above the level of any preceding post-war year.
Then another excerpt from the report:
Since this was written a large number of returns from the July survey have been received. Eighty per cent of the industries have revised their employment forecasts downward over the past three months, with the downward revision of total employment being about 2 per cent.
The estimate of average unemployment for 1958 as forecast in the "Canadian Economic Outlook" was 425,000, an increase of 67 per cent over 1957. I ask the minister whether he thinks this figure is too high. If he does, undoubtedly he will tell us and it will be a reassuring statement from him. But does he really think this 67 per cent increase over 1957 is too high when for the first six months of 1958 the percentage of unemployed on the average has been 72.6 per cent higher than for the corresponding period of 1957? If the

minister feels that the figure of 67 per cent as an average over the year is not too high, it represents a serious situation which challenges all of us to do something about it, and which certainly challenges the government. Before this item is carried, perhaps the minister will tell us what the government proposes to do about it.
Before answering these questions, the minister might like to recall again what he and his colleagues used to say about unemployment when they were in opposition and during the election campaign. Before I sit down I should like to refer him to a statement attributed to him in the Winnipeg Free Press of March 5, 1958, in these words:
It is our duty to see that no Canadian suffers a single loss of a job this year.
If the minister finds some difficulty in telling us how the government is going to meet this responsibility, and I can understand the difficulty for it is certainly not an easy problem, perhaps he might discuss this issue with his colleague the Secretary of State for External Affairs. I know he is engaged on important work in New York at the moment, but during the election campaign the Secretary of State for External Affairs had a very simple solution to the unemployment problem, because the Saskatchewan Star-Phoenix of March 15 reports him in this way:
External affairs minister Sidney Smith told a Saskatoon audience Friday evening, jobs were the immediate solution to unemployment in Canada.
There is no doubt that is true. Jobs are certainly the answer to the jobless, but what are the policies of the government which it is hoped will provide these jobs in the months ahead? It is the answer to that question that we would like to get. We would at least like to hear from the minister on that question before this estimate is passed.

maintopic: EMPLOYMENT AND UNEMPLOYMENT IN CANADA FOR THE FIRST SIX MONTHS OF 1957 AND 1958
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to address myself for a few moments to one phase of the minister's opening statement which over the years has not, in my humble opinion, received the attention from parliament that it deserves. I want to speak for a few moments about our vocational training program. In his opening statement the minister announced to the house, and I have also noted in the report of the director of vocational training, that $40 million is being set aside for vocational training in the coming year, but the strange thing is that of that amount $25 million is being devoted to capital assistance toward the building and equipment of schools and only $15 million for training and education.
I consider that for a country like Canada $15 million for training our youth in trades
57071-3-2281
Supply-Labour
in technical schools is indeed a very paltry amount, and it is distributed amongst the provinces of Canada to such an extent that it cannot really make a serious impression in any province. To me it appears to be somewhat of an excuse for us to be able to say that we are doing something about vocational training. It is like going over a subject once very lightly.
In my opinion the problem is certainly deserving of much more serious attention. It is a national problem, and if the minister and his officials will really think deeply about it I believe they will come to the conclusion that we have sort of been glossing over it. I think we have been delinquent in training our people to keep abreast of technological improvements, automation and inventions in all industries, and unless our workers are trained to keep up with the progress of the times our industries will fall very far behind.
It is true that some contributions are made. I do not know why some provinces insist on thinking of this matter in terms of education and refuse certain subsidies, as some provinces have refused them. This matter too might fall under the heading of education. I would address myself to hon. gentlemen in the province of Quebec and ask them to consider seriously this matter of whether we are not delinquent in the province of Quebec in the matter of the training we are giving, realizing of course that education falls entirely within the jurisdiction of the province. However, this is something that falls under the heading of labour. Unless we are going to train our youth and give them facilities with which to keep abreast of the modern advances of science, certainly our skilled labour will be falling far behind.
I should like to suggest to the minister- and this is a humble suggestion-that the Department of Labour, under his guidance, create in Canada one central training institute where we will train not necessarily skilled labour but teachers. We should have a vocational teachers' training institute so that the very best teachers trained in the central school may go to the different provinces and the different institutes. There, with their training as skilled teachers, they may be able to do a much better job than is being done now.
What happens at the present time? The technical schools or the trade schools in the various provinces call in individuals who may be excellent craftsmen. They may be excellent in their own industry but they are not necessarily good pedagogues; they are not necessarily good teachers. I do not think they have the fullest ability to get across to pupils in the way a trained pedagogue can.

Supply-Labour
If the Department of Labour would take a proper view of vocational training in Canada much could be done. Of course, as I said before, I consider its present program merely an excuse for saying "We are doing something about it". Actually I think we would blush if we compared our efforts in the matter of vocational training with the effort of other countries. Very respectfully and seriously I suggest to the Minister of Labour that here is an opportunity to develop in Canada a program of vocational training, not only by going into the provinces with petty subsidies as we are doing now but by creating an institute for teachers.
I happen to know something about the matter because I am connected with a vocational training organization with schools in various countries in the world. I speak from some experience. That organization has a teacher training institute set up in Geneva. What they do there is train people. The graduates of that institute then travel to various countries and to the various schools. They are expert teachers in vocational training. I think this step would be welcomed by industry in Canada. I feel confident, and I think the minister will agree with me, that industry in Canada could benefit from more skilled labour. I do not know how many hundreds or how many thousands of these skilled technicians from other countries are now in Canada working on Canadian projects.
I do not deride this fact. I think they are necessary. I think they are doing a magnificent job for industry in Canada, but why should we not have our own people trained to do that work? Labour would welcome it. I feel certain that labour would subsidize such a central teachers institute. Labour certainly would create bursaries and scholarships and encourage it in every possible way, if approached, because it is to their benefit. Industry is seeking trained help. Shortly after the war there was a dearth of trained labour in the country and the minister will recall that we sent team after team-I refer to Canadian teams-over to Europe in order to seek out skilled labour there.
Whilst we have been following a program of vocational training in Canada, I direct my appeal again to the minister to think very seriously about this project of creating in Canada an institute for teachers of vocational training. We have, for example, schools or institutes in which we train teachers to go into the elementary schools to teach our children. They are trained teachers; they are trained pedagogues. We have institutes in which we train people to enter the universities in order to train our people in the higher

fields of education. But in the field of vocational training or technical training we have been greatly delinquent.
I do not lay this fault at the feet of the present administration; past administrations must certainly assume some responsibility. But I really think now is the time, when Canada has grown up, to take this step. We need a great deal of skilled labour in Canada. We cannot get it, Mr. Chairman, to the extent that we shall require it unless we create an institute that will train the appropriate teachers to go back into our various provinces, since they control the vocational training schools, where they will qualify our people for that service.

maintopic: EMPLOYMENT AND UNEMPLOYMENT IN CANADA FOR THE FIRST SIX MONTHS OF 1957 AND 1958
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am pleased to associate myself with what I understood to be the recommendation of the hon. member for Cartier. Having been connected with education for a number of years in Canada I have long realized the need for a training school for our technical teachers. The atmosphere that would prevail at such a training school varies so much from the regular academic normal schools that I think the proposal put forward by the hon. member, namely that we establish at least one national training school for vocational teachers, is worthy of the most serious consideration. I believe it would greatly assist in supplying those teachers which at the present time are in meagre numbers.
I should like to congratulate the minister
__this is the first occasion on which I have
had the opportunity to make any reference to him-on his attitude since becoming Minister of Labour. He has always been extremely modest. He is one cabinet minister that you can expect to find almost anywhere in Ottawa. He lives with the people whom he professes to serve. He makes a great effort to maintain contact with the ordinary taxpayers of Canada. I feel that his example might well be emulated by other cabinet ministers. With his approach to human beings and human problems, how in the world he finds himself in the ranks of the Conservative party is something I have never been quite able to figure out. However, he is there and I know that his presence will be an influence for good.
I hope the Minister of Labour will not look upon everything we say as his own personal and sole measure of responsibility. I have always regretted-and I said this previously when Hon. Milton Gregg was minister-that we seem to throw all the blame for unemployment on whoever happens to the Minister of Labour, whereas actually unemployment as such is more the major concern of the cabinet as a whole, including

such men as the Minister of Finance, the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Minister of Agriculture. These men actually have more to do with the level of employment in the nation. Yet somehow or other the Minister of Labour is the minister whose estimates are before us when we talk about unemployment, and he always has to take it in the neck for whatever is wrong in the employment field.
Partly to refresh the minister's memory, I would like to refer to an article which appeared in the Montreal Gazette of October 17, 1957. As the minister will remember, that was shortly after the house opened and when he first became Minister of Labour. The headline was "Job Threat Met", and the article read as follows:
Labour minister Starr was ready in the commons when Erhart Eegier (C.C.F.-Burnaby-Coquitlam) asked what steps the government is taking to alleviate "a rapidly growing unemployment problem".
In quick succession, Mr. Starr listed what the new Progressive Conservative government has done:
1.	The government has started up its strive for a greater construction program.
2.	National employment service offices have been ordered to step up the tempo of finding jobs for the unemployed.
3.	Immigration for the rest of the year has been curtailed because of pressure on the national labour force caused by the heavy influx earlier this year.
4.	The government has made available $150,000,000 for a housing loans fund.
I had the feeling at that time that this was not nearly adequate and that the newspaper reporter had been indeed optimistic when he analysed this as meeting the job threat. I am sure many other members in this house were afraid that this would not nearly meet the situation.
The government did make efforts to help by means of the winter construction program, and I suppose the government and the minister may argue that if this four-point program had not been pursued last winter unemployment in Canada would have been much worse. That, to me, is a very, very weak argument to use as an apology for the serious level of unemployment which even now exists in the middle of our summer, when we normally have next to no unemployment at all.
I know that the national employment service officers were ordered to bestir themselves and look for possible openings for our unemployed. However, both the first and second measures are very hard to analyse, and I do not think even the minister would be able to tell us with any accuracy how much employment was actually created by those policies.
With respect to the third policy, the curtailing of immigration for the rest of the year,
Supply-Labour
I have never been exactly convinced that immigration adds to unemployment. I agree that the unplanned immigration which we had for many years did aggravate the situation in that such a very heavy percentage- sometimes as high as 65 per cent-of the immigrants were single men ready and willing to take employment. I notice, however, that even today the minister's colleague is still pursuing a policy of allowing able workers to come to the country provided they are sponsored by someone in Canada, while at the same time she denies entry to Canada of consumers and future citizens such as the type of people I have referred to as the orphans of the world. Canadians even today are not allowed to bring from other parts of the world, orphans whom they wish to adopt and who certainly would not be a threat to those presently employed in our country. I do not think that answer has met the situation, therefore.
I will agree, however, that the fourth policy has done very much to help the situation. The money this government has made available for housing and the further funds made available under this section I must admit have helped us very, very much.
We do get the impression that this government, by deliberate design, has decided to try to ride out the storm. No policies have yet been advanced, by this minister or indeed by any other minister or by the Prime Minister himself, whereby the government is consciously embarking upon a program to lick once and for all this problem of unemployment which seems to bedevil so many of the western nations. Even assuming that economic conditions were to take a turn for the better, and that thereby in one respect the government is able to ride out the storm, I submit, and we have long submitted in this party, that the problem caused by automation is going to prevent us from eliminating the recurring problem of unemployment, and that if we ride out this present economic recession automation will assume even greater proportions which will require measures to be adopted.
The Leader of the Opposition made some reference to governmental assurances in the past that the problem of unemployment had been largely overcome and that we had every reason to look forward to sunnier days ahead. I was looking through my notes over the lunch hour and, though I did not bring them with me, I found in them many references to occasions when the former minister of labour, for instance in 1954, was assuring the Canadian public that as far as unemployment insurance and unemployment generally were concerned we were over the

Supply-Labour
hump. That is rather old phraseology, and I wish responsible ministers would not use it so often; because it leads to a certain cynicism in the hearts of the unemployed in Canada when they read these statements.
I know the minister is not the first minister to place very great reliance upon statistics supplied to him by the officers of his department, but I would like to point out that those figures for last winter indicated some three-quarters of a million unemployed. Another set of figures showed a much lower total. I submit, and I have always submitted, that even the worst figures supplied to the minister are not adequate to show the situation, and in this regard I would like to place on record the problem which was brought forward by the Ontario welfare council in their submission to the then prime minister of Canada on January 28, 1955. Among other things they referred to approximately 20 per cent of the labour force not being covered by unemployment insurance, and they took the figure of
750.000	unemployed. When you add 20 per cent to that figure-because they have no reason to go to the offices of the unemployment insurance commission since they are not registered and are not eligible-you get an additional 150,000, and that figure of
750.00	becomes 900,000. Those people are unprotected against need arising out of unemployment, and number approximately one-quarter as many as are covered.
Then there is another class of persons, namely those whose benefits have expired. This group, I think, is particularly pertinent at this time when the minister supplies us with figures relating to the number of our unemployed. There are thousands of Canadians who no longer have any need to go near the offices of the unemployment insurance commission because they have nothing to gain. These are the people whose benefits have expired. It is apparent that at a time when the unemployment situation has worsened steadily many people have used up their right to benefit under the provisions of the Unemployment Insurance Act. Supplementary benefits in the winter months only partially meet the need.
Another class of people who are not really on record are those persons without sufficient credits to entitle them to claim insurance benefits; young people entering the labour market, newcomers to Canada and others who are unprotected because they have not worked long enough to become entitled to benefits. There is also the class of people whose benefits are not sufficient to enable them to support themselves and their families at even a minimum subsistence level.

They would not add to the official figures, but the other categories would, and they should be borne in mind when we are considering the statistics on unemployment.
We were given the assurance-I do not recall its precise terms-that as long as the present government is in office, or as long as the present Prime Minister is in office, the Canadian people can be assured that no one will suffer as a result of unemployment. That was a very odd announcement at the time it was made. If we consider that the maximum that is payable to an unemployed person under the Unemployment Insurance Act is some $30 a week for a man with a family, and that in many cases he has payments to make on the first mortgage on his home and often on a second mortgage; or, failing that, in rent; and that he has payments to make on his furniture and possibly on an automobile, as well as his ordinary costs of upkeep such as the weekly food bill, clothing bills, medical bills and so on, I cannot accept the assurance that no one will suffer because of unemployment as long as the present government remains in office, if at the same time all this government has to offer the unemployed is this maximum of $30-odd a week.
I should like to ask the minister whether he does not think it is about time we should consider removing that ceiling, or raising it, with regard to the maximum amounts that are payable under the Unemployment Insurance Act. This becomes especially important when people are unemployed for any length of time. I suppose all of us, for a month or for two or three months, could manage to live somehow on $30 a week. However, there are many Canadians who have had to live on that small amount of money for six, seven or eight months, and others who are no longer able to get even this help.
The situation is much more serious than the announcements of the government like to make out, and unless some action is taken now I am making the prediction that next winter will see over one million unemployed in Canada. And quite apart from the human suffering that will be caused when this takes place, if we consider the loss to the nation of having a million men unemployed in our country for a period of a year, we find that it means a loss in production, a loss in the wealth of our people, of three billion dollars or in other words 10 per cent of our present gross national product. That 10 per cent is far more than enough to spell either prosperity or depression for our people.
We feel that the government is not paying enough attention to the seriousness of the

problem. I know that the minister himself is spending a great deal of time on it, and what I have to say deals with the minister's representations to the cabinet. I hope when he attends cabinet meetings he is not the mild and meek man we meet on the sidewalks or in the lobbies of the hotels in Ottawa, or wherever we meet him. I hope he is much more aggressive, and that he will become a front bench member of the cabinet. I could never understand why the Minister of Labour has to occupy a seat in the second row, because labour is the most important single element in our society and the Minister of Labour deserves a seat close to the Prime Minister himself.
I listened to the Leader of the Opposition, and I noticed that while he found some fault with the government's optimism he did not offer very many remedies as to how employment might be provided. Maybe this is not the time to go into details on that particular question, but I had been hoping he would go into somewhat more detail than he did. Of course the answer to unemployment is increased markets for Canadian goods. This involves greater international trade. We have to extend our program of economic aid abroad; we have to see that the people who make up the labour force receive a fair return so they are able to buy back what they make, and that agriculture is given a fair purchasing power in our economy.
It is amazing to me that wherever you have a planned economy-and I am not referring now to nations behind the iron curtain-where-ever you have a government in the western world consciously embarking on a planned economy, you have licked the problem of unemployment. As long as there is conscious planning on the part of a government, unemployment is a relatively easy matter to deal with. If people insist on continuing the economic set-up which they are now perpetuating they will have to adopt the policy that if a man is unemployed he is entitled to unemployment insurance benefits until employment is found for him without any limitation in terms of weeks or months, and to this end supplementary benefits should be payable the year round.
I know this will mean payments out of consolidated revenue, because at the present rate of expenditure, according to the figures which were placed on record at page 2137 of Hansard, we find that at the rate of depletion as it obtained in January and February of this year the fund would only last for 16 months before it was exhausted. Thus, if we are going to extend either the size of the payment or the length of time during which payments may be made, the government will
Supply-Labour
have to revise the financial set-up of the unemployment insurance fund.
I should also like to suggest to the minister that he recommend the setting up of many more offices in the urban parts of Canada. One of the cruelest things which apply to a man who is unemployed is the fact that he has to stand in this line-up sometimes two or three blocks long. In the wintertime he has to stand in the snow or rain to obtain his meal ticket, or to register, or to do whatever it is he needs to do, and I think the minister would earn our gratitude by telling the senior officials in his department, "look, we do not care to build for you a huge organization with a six or seven floor office building with hundreds of civil servants at your command. In the city of Vancouver we want 12 or 15 insurance offices so there may be a human touch, and so the unemployed may not become mere cogs in a machine." If that were done I think not only would more employment be found through these offices, but in addition the unemployed themselves would not have to suffer the terrible humiliation they now feel when they are almost like prisoners in a penitentiary, when in fact all they have is a number.
In fact, in some of these huge offices costing millions of dollars of the taxpayers' money they have become so arrogant that they keep locked the doors of the washrooms lest some unemployed throw a paper towel on the floor and whoever looks after the building would have to pick up that piece of waste paper. I think it is mean to insist that people stand for hours in line without having access to washroom facilities when such facilities are already available in the building and were installed for the purpose of handling the people who have business to do in the building.
I also wish the minister would use his influence to obtain far more money for the adult education program particularly as it applies to vocational training. I would appreciate it if the minister in his reply would indicate how much of the money is estimated for each of the ten provinces. I believe the hon. member for Cartier expressed regret over the fact that not all of the provinces were taking advantage of the aid available for technical education. If my memory serves me correctly his province takes a larger share of the available assistance than does any other province and I should like to congratulate the people of the province of Quebec on that attitude. With respect to retraining workers and providing technical education the people of that province have not hesitated to play their full role.

Supply-Labour
The problem of adult education is very important and with the development of automation it is going to become a much more serious problem. The department is expending $71 million this year through the unemployment insurance commission branch but only $7 million is being expended for vocational education. They are spending ten times as much to supply relief which in the long run is only a stop-gap action as they are spending to supply technical and vocational training that will assist workers to play a useful role in society. Making more money available for this kind of training and building more institutions for this purpose will assist in solving the problem.
We have reached the point where men of 35 and 40 years of age have to learn new trades because of automation. Many of these men are married and have family responsibilities. We cannot expect them to take a technical course for a six-month period and leave their families without means of sustenance. We will have to enhance our program of aid for those who take the courses and assume responsibility for the incomes of the families while the breadwinners are learning to equip themselves for new roles in life.
I hope the minister will also pay some attention to a growing problem in Canada. I know he did not like what he felt he had to do in the case of a public utility on the west coast but I believe the time has come when the federal government should take the leadership and begin to sit down with Canadian organized labour to see whether in the field of public utilities a solution cannot be found that will be acceptable both to those owning public utilities and to the workers involved. None of us wants compulsory arbitration I am sure and yet that is apparently what will come about because of the way we are allowing things to go on at the present time. As time goes on that situation will become worse. The minister with his kindly and conciliatory nature through his department would be able to supply a real service to the Canadian labour scene if he would offer leadership in that direction.

maintopic: EMPLOYMENT AND UNEMPLOYMENT IN CANADA FOR THE FIRST SIX MONTHS OF 1957 AND 1958
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in rising to take part in this debate on the first item of the estimates of the Department of Labour I must admit at the very outset I find myself in a very difficult position mainly because of my personal affection and high regard for the Minister of Labour. I believe the Dominion of Canada over the last years has been . highly fortunate in its choice of those who have filled that very important portfolio. Certainly the life and accomplishments of the late Humphrey Mitchell will live in our

memories for many years. The Hon. Milton F. Gregg performed a fine job in the capacity of minister of labour and although perhaps he has jumped from the frying pan into the fire we will not forget what he accomplished on behalf of the working class people of this country. And now we have the present genial Minister of Labour.
I must admit I admire the hon. gentleman for more than one reason. One of the main reasons for my admiration of him, and I think it was mentioned on other occasions, is that he is fair and square and when asked a question he does not give a political answer. I have always felt it was a pleasure to ask him questions in the house because he does not throw the question back to the Liberal party and attempt to place the blame on the previous administration for whatever condition is being discussed. He does not try to make us believe we are at fault for every situation that arises. When he is at fault he accepts the blame like a man and does not behave like some other ministers who attempt to throw the blame on the past Liberal regime.
The minister is to be congratulated, too, because he has a very fine group of officials in his department. If I may use the parlance of the baseball field, no manager can be successful unless he has a good bench. The minister is certainly fortunate because he has a good bench, a highly competent group of officials standing behind him. I have always felt that no minister of the crown could do a good job unless he had capable officials assisting him. I had an opportunity to observe the work of these officials when serving on the industrial relations committee and was greatly impressed when they presented their brief to the committee and answered questions concerning the operations of the department. I say to the minister that both he and his officials deserve a great deal of credit.
Another thing I like about the minister, and the previous speaker referred to it as well, is that he always wears a friendly smile. We always like to see him in the building because of his cheerful countenance although we did miss him during the six weeks when he was attending the labour conference in Geneva. Another thing about the minister that will stand out permanently in the minds of all hon. members is that when he was in opposition he was Mike to everybody and now that he has been elevated to the high position he holds he is still the same old Mike and we love him for the many fine personal qualities he has.
I have thrown orchids to the minister and as a member of Her Majesty's loyal opposition I presume I may now be allowed to

throw bean balls, to use another baseball expression. I am advised that there is a new rule in baseball. An umpire has the right to fine a pitcher $50 for throwing a bean ball. Mr. Chairman, if you feel I am throwing a bean ball, simply call it to my attention and I shall desist from doing so.
During the last election campaign, as was referred to by my leader and the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam, the Prime Minister stated that should a Conservative government be returned on March 31-and it certainly was returned with an overwhelming majority-"no Canadian shall suffer through unemployment". Those were the words he used. This promise, reflecting as it did the great public concern over the deepening crisis in our economy was largely responsible for the unprecedented mandate the Conservative party received from the Canadian people. Many families suffering real hardship as a result of extended unemployment expect the Prime Minister to fulfil his promise. It is the opinion, based on experience and fortified by studies of Canadian and United States economists, that the present crisis is not of a seasonable nature but is beginning to take on the deep-going and all-embracing nature of that of the thirties.
The vast unemployed wealth of our country stands indeed in sharp contrast to the presence of over half a million workers who want desperately to be gainfully employed, but for whom no work is to be found. Similarly, vast surpluses in consumer goods piling up in warehouses from coast to coast stand in sharp contrast to real hardship experienced by hundreds of thousands of Canadian families who have been unwillingly removed as a market for these products by unemployment.
We feel that only by extraordinary measures on the part of the federal administration can these contradictions be corrected. And by "we" I mean the Liberal party. I refer to measures which will result in extensive public spending in projects of a nationbuilding character, measures which will open the markets of the world for our industrial and farm products, measures which will place more consumer purchasing power in the hands of the unemployed, thus achieving the twofold purpose of increasing the home market for our surpluses while guaranteeing that no unemployed worker or his family shall suffer through unemployment.
Certainly, no feature of America's economic life-and when I say "America" I am including the United States and Canada- has been more at the heart of our rapidly rising and widely shared levels than the daring of this nation's businesses in pricing for volume and taking their chances on profit.
57071-3-229
Supply-Labour
It is no accident that this policy has characterized our most profitable industries. If we are to maintain the vigour and vitality of our free economy this drive for the widest possible markets must continue. A price policy designed to bring increasing volume should be nothing short of an article of faith for every businessman. The economic recovery and growth we bring about must take the form, not of higher costs and prices but of more production and more jobs.
We might just as well be realistic over this trouble. If we as earners obtain such large increases in our incomes each year that the cost of production moves always upward, then as customers we shall find only higher price tags on the goods in the stores.
The Canadian people believe in good wages, both in private and public employment. Good wages reward effort and build markets. But the Canadian people are going to be looking over the shoulders of those sitting at every bargaining table to see whether the wage settlement and subsequent price decisions are consistent with a stable dollar, or whether they mean another dismal sequence of ever-rising costs and prices. Inequities in the wage structure must, of course, be adjusted. But consumers are not going to be satisfied with less and less value per dollar of price, which is the inevitable result of less and less production per dollar of cost. If businessmen and labour union leaders forget these truths, the consumers will remind them in ways that are clear and painful and, in the process, the whole economy will suffer. These are not theoretical considerations; they have a direct bearing on specific industries today.
I was impressed-and the Minister of Labour spoke about it when he introduced his estimates this morning-about the older people and the lack of employment. Mr. Robert Scott, executive secretary of the Alberta federation of labour, said this, and I think it is very important:
Age discrimination is one of the most serious unemployment problems in industry today. It has aggravated the general jobless situation across Canada.
He continued:
Employers are considering workers over 40 years of age obsolete. In some cases persons who are 35 are too old to be employed.
He went on to say:
These people are forgetting that in general workers are more efficient and dependable between the ages of 40 and 50.
Dr. F. W. Hanley of Calgary said this. He has studied the problem:
Probably never before has the aging man so frequently been denied an opportunity to exchange his work for the essentials of living.

Supply-Labour
much some of the proponents of the idea will groan if it causes an increase in their income tax. With the government engaged in a large public works program it is indeed reasonable that it should see that as much as possible is done in the winter. But it is also reasonable, and I am very emphatic about this, that industry should try to remain in production throughout the year instead of operating on the basis of six months of overtime and six months of lay-offs. It is not only the government but business that should start long range planning to prevent another great winter slump.
The years since the end of the second world war saw a constant increase in employment. The rising tide was not checked until the middle of 1957 and as the government changed at that time it was natural that many people should blame the Progressive Conservative party. Whether or not they are right I am not going to judge. It is a question for a master economist, but actually we had gone a long time without a recession of any considerable size.
During the warmer months employment has been gradually increasing but the fact remains that the situation is still bad for this season of the year. With the automobile industry in a great slump, many of the firms that supply mechanical parts, glass, tires and other materials and many that supply the tools and machinery for automotive construction are also under pressure. Indeed, many western farmers, as members from the west know, are looking out at barren and drought-parched land and are facing one of the poorest harvests. That will certainly not aid the employment situation next winter.
I should like to say a word or two about the dispute between the 15 unions representing the non-operating personnel and the Canadian railways. The settlement of this dispute is indeed of great national importance. Apart from the establishment of rates of pay and working conditions for this segment of the railway industry, the settlement will also have an impact on the wages and working conditions of all railway employees. We all know that the settlement of other union contracts within the railway industry depends upon the settlement which is reached in the dispute between the companies and the unions representing the non-operating personnel. The settlement will also have an impact upon the general economy of the country through the ultimate cost of rail service.
What has happened to date? Last November, almost ten months ago, the unions submitted their proposals and demands to form the basis of a new agreement to replace the contract which was to expire on December

31, 1957. The unions, representing approximately 127,000 employees of the two major railways alone, proposed that the wages of their members be increased as of January 1 of this year by 11 per cent plus 17 cents an hour. In addition, the unions proposed other revisions of the then existing contract, the most important of which had to do with the health and welfare plan, to which the railways were asked to double their contribution, and the request for a more generous vacation policy.
Since the unions tabled their demands last November the normal process of collective bargaining has been followed. The unions and the companies failed after a little more than three weeks to reach any basis for settlement. At the request of the unions the Minister of Labour established a conciliation board on December 2. Little progress was made until the board commenced its hearings on March 3 in Montreal. We know that the delay was due in part to a protest by the union over the appointment of the chairman of the board who, after a month, resigned. However, that delay was unfortunate, and perhaps unnecessary, as the Minister of Labour could have learned, before the appointment was made, whether either party had valid reservations about the nominee. This delay not only caused inconvenience to the parties to the dispute but also seriously retarded the ultimate settlement of the dispute upon which so much depends both within and without the industry.
The board has now submitted reports to the minister and to the parties. These reports are dated July 21 and were made public on the 30th of last month. Since then we have had no further word on what progress has been made or what steps have been taken to bring about a settlement.
We know that the chairman of the board and the representative of the union submitted a joint report which the minister has stated is to be considered the report of the board, in which an increase in wages was recommended. The increases are as follows: four cents an hour retroactive to January 1 of this year; an additional three per cent effective the first of next month; and a third increase of three per cent to be effective April 1, 1959. The representative of the companies in his minority report recommended no changes in the wage rates for the year of 1958. The members of the board also commented on the other issues in the dispute but I do not propose to mention them at this time. However, I propose to ask the minister what his department and the government proposes to do now with regard to this problem. The conciliation process has now been exhausted.

The parties may accept or reject the majority report of the board and they are free to follow whatever course they choose from that time onward.
We on this side of the house-and I say this to the Minister of Labour-know that it is not an easy task for the government to face, that it is not easy to bring about a settlement which provides for the employees rates of pay and working conditions comparable with those paid for similar work and which, at the same time, does not place an unreasonable strain on the resources of the companies. But if the dispute is to be solved, imaginative and bold action must be undertaken by the government right now. The dispute cannot be allowed to drift until the environment has become so muddied that a solution cannot be found without causing great inconvenience to the country and its economy or by other drastic measures.
I want to say this, Mr. Chairman. In opposition the minister-and the minister was not too pronounced in this matter-and his colleagues made daring and bold statements about how they, if they were in power, would deal with such disputes; how they would solve these disputes within the framework of collective bargaining and with a minimum of delay. The Prime Minister and other members of the present government were bitter in their comments about the slowness of the Liberal government in dealing with such disputes and they made sweeping charges about the government's ineffectiveness. I am going to ask the minister and the government what they are going to do about it.
I think the Minister of Labour is duty bound to tell this house and the nation what steps he is taking or proposes to take to bring about a settlement without a strike or a forced settlement by legislation. What is the government doing to prevent this dispute degenerating into a second British Columbia coastal steamship episode?
If I may, Mr. Chairman, I should just like to bring to the attention of the Minister of Labour a local problem and ask the indulgence of hon. members of the house for another few minutes. I have received a complaint-and I think it is one that is justified -concerning the fact that United States musicians are allowed to enter Canada for the purpose of playing musical engagements, whereas Canadians are stopped by United States immigration officers from taking performing jobs in the United States. Meetings have been held not only in Niagara Falls but in other places along the border by the various locals. Our own local union passed a resolution to write to the Minister of Labour protesting the ease with which United States
Supply-Labour
musicians are allowed to enter Canada. A reply to this resolution was received from the deputy minister of labour, Mr. A. H. Brown, in which he states in the last paragraph of it;
If you know of any cases of musicians who have entered Canada under section 7G for the purpose
of giving specific performances and have remained in Canada to accept regular employment or persons who have entered Canada under permit to accept the position which could be filled by a resident in Canada.
We have a number of members in our local in Niagara Falls who have been out of work this past winter and spring and many of them have been working on short time. Their membership is quite excited to think that in all cases they could have very capably filled the requests for professional musicians that have been so frequently filled by men from across the border who seem to be lucky enough, according to their contracts, to be able to secure work in Canada at almost double the price which people pay for Canadian musicians. I have learned just recently that these musicians from the United States come over without even bonding their instruments. I am asking the minister to give the matter some attention. I know it is a question of customs. I hope he will take the matter up with the minister concerned and see whether something cannot be done. Each and every time one of our Canadian musicians attempts to go across with his instruments to engage in a playing job in Niagara Falls or Buffalo, he is always told by the United States immigration officers, "You can't come in for you would only take jobs away from United States musicians". Fair play is fair play. I know the minister will do something about that problem.
Might I sum up, Mr. Chairman, by saying this.

speechtext: Agreed.

maintopic: EMPLOYMENT AND UNEMPLOYMENT IN CANADA FOR THE FIRST SIX MONTHS OF 1957 AND 1958
speechtext:
Thank you. I can only sum up what I have been trying to say in this way. The government must do something and do it immediately. Certainly the Canadian people look to this government to take the lead first by creating new purchasing power, by drastically reducing income and sales tax immediately, raising income tax exemptions for single persons and in a much higher

Supply-Labour
bracket for married persons with dependent children. Second, in expanding employment by a new trade policy, by seeking increased trade on the basis of mutual advantage with other countries. Third, the economy could be primed by construction of thousands of new homes and extended public works should be brought forward to build needed schools, hospitals, highways, power and irrigation projects. Fourth, the needs of the unemployed must be met by an increase in unemployment benefits, these benefits to continue for a longer time of unemployment.
Might I say this, Mr. Chairman, and I do this seriously indeed. If the people of Canada had followed the Liberal platform in the last election and indeed the Pearson plan, namely a vacation on taxation, and placing the dollar back into circulation, certainly we would not be facing the serious unemployment situation we are facing at the present time.

maintopic: EMPLOYMENT AND UNEMPLOYMENT IN CANADA FOR THE FIRST SIX MONTHS OF 1957 AND 1958
speechtext:
In rising, Mr. Chairman, to participate in the discussion of this particular vote, I would like, as the hon. members have done, to make a comment or two with respect to the minister himself as an individual and with respect to the attitude that he has shown both in the house in dealing with questions, by correspondence and in personal discussions. I have the highest commendation for the minister for the sincerity that he shows, and for the humbleness that is apparent in his everyday dealings with the problems of his department. I know that it is not because of lack of sincerity or lack of desire on his part if the other cabinet ministers do not agree with him in some of the proposals that he may make from time to time. However, I would suggest that there are some other cabinet ministers, notably the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Agriculture, who would be well advised to follow the attitude and the example set by the Minister of Labour. If they would do so, I am sure that we would be able to conduct the discussions relating to their respective departments with the same degree of amicability and sensibility that we are able to discuss the questions relating to the department of the Minister of Labour.
I have listened with a great deal of interest to the opinions expressed by the Leader of the Opposition in his opening remarks on this vote, because I wondered whether the Liberal party was going to exhibit any different attitude today from that which they adopted while in office during the past years. All I could discover, however, was the same exhibition of verbal wandering into the question of labour-management relations, a

subject with which he is not too familiar. However, the Leader of the Opposition ably and succinctly posed the problem in a nutshell when he dealt with the solution to unemployment. In posing that problem he included in his comments an observation of the Secretary of State for External Affairs in a speech made by that gentleman, I believe, at Saskatoon, when he said that the solution to unemployment is jobs. Of course I quite agree with both these hon. gentlemen in that connection and apparently there is at least one thing which one will learn if one spends some time in the Department of External Affairs; one can at least get to know what the problem is even if one has no idea of the solution to it. One of the first realizations one would have, apparently, would be the realization of the right questions to ask.
I know that in dealing with the estimates of the Department of Labour we could, and probably will, expand our discussions beyond the actual field covered by the department. We could get into the internal operations and attitudes of the unions and of management and the relationships between the two groups and the impact of those organizations upon society. It is not my intention to wander into any specific aspect of that field or to refer to specific elements of society, but even though I may have some pretty definite opinions on the attitude of management, I will confine my remarks to a few comments concerning the unions themselves. This is because I spent a number of years as an officer of unions and a certain period as an officer of one particular union, and as a result of this experience I came to know something of the day to day working within the unions.
Firstly I must say that in Canada we are in nowhere near the position in which the United States finds itself with respect to some of the unions south of the border. The situation in respect of those unions has been well publicized by certain United States senate investigation committees, and my personal opinion is that as a whole we have a much cleaner group of unions in Canada than exists in the United States.

maintopic: EMPLOYMENT AND UNEMPLOYMENT IN CANADA FOR THE FIRST SIX MONTHS OF 1957 AND 1958
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: EMPLOYMENT AND UNEMPLOYMENT IN CANADA FOR THE FIRST SIX MONTHS OF 1957 AND 1958
speechtext:
I say that, knowing as I do many of the union officials in this country. There are, however, some Canadian unions whose policies and operations certainly do not fit within the expression of opinion I have just voiced. I have personal knowledge of some unions where the members are absolutely afraid of losing their membership cards and of losing their jobs as a result of expressing their opinions at union meetings. This is a most deplorable state of affairs in what is supposed to be a free society and

where people are supposed to be able to express their opinions, be they critical or in commendation. Because of the operations of some Canadian unions, however, such freedom of expression does not exist although these unions are in the minority.
Unless this situation is cleaned up with respect to particular unions there is a danger of such practices extending to other unions and, although I hope I will never live to see the day when this happens, the unions may fall into such disfavour among their own members and with the public in general that the Canadian people may decide some corrective legislative steps will have to be taken.

maintopic: EMPLOYMENT AND UNEMPLOYMENT IN CANADA FOR THE FIRST SIX MONTHS OF 1957 AND 1958
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question? Would he care to mention the particular unions he has in mind?

maintopic: EMPLOYMENT AND UNEMPLOYMENT IN CANADA FOR THE FIRST SIX MONTHS OF 1957 AND 1958
speechtext:
No, I will not mention the particular unions I have in mind because, as I stated earlier, I do not think this falls within the jurisdiction of the Department of Labour. I merely express these views in a general way. It might be said that I am hiding behind the question, but I would rather not give the names of individual unions about which I have personal knowledge. I hope that will satisfy the questioner.
As I said earlier, however, only a small fraction of the total of millions of Canadian members are affected in this way. I do not think the inference should be drawn from my remarks, and I am sure it could not be drawn, that within the unions to which I have referred the same sort of thing exists as apparently exists in certain United States unions which have now come under the surveillance of the senate investigation committee. I refer to racketeering, thugs and gangsters who get control of the unions for their own immediate ends. I am certainly not implying that such is the situation here but, as I say, I have personal knowledge of some policies being followed in Canadian unions which have the effect of placing union members in fear of losing their jobs so that they will not express their opinions on union policies.
I wish to raise another point which comes more specifically within the ambit of the department's jurisdiction, and this has to do with the reference which has been made to the operative machinery used for negotiations, that is to say the process of direct bargaining, the use of conciliation officers and conciliation boards and, in some cases, what I believe are called industrial inquiry commissions. With respect to the legislative or operative machinery for negotiation, I wish to express some thoughts I outlined in discussing a particular bill a few weeks ago.
Supply-Labour
We have in Canada a most ridiculous situation with respect to our labour laws applying to negotiations and relationships between union and management in collective bargaining. We have a federal act which embraces certain employees across the nation, but ten of our provinces are concerned with the field of labour legislation with respect to matters falling under the jurisdiction of the provinces themselves. All in all, we have or could have, eleven different types of legislation for the certification of unions, eleven different types of legislation for the granting of bargaining rights, eleven different types of legislation so far as conciliation procedures are concerned and eleven different types of legislation regarding the entire field of labour-management relations from the original moment of organizing to the final signing of the collective agreement.
It is neither sensible nor conducive to efficiency to have this diversity or this difference of legislation. In some cases the unions find themselves operating under one set of bargaining procedures as laid down by law, while just across the border in a neighbouring province the same union and the same employer might find themselves covered by a different set of laws. In the federal field the same thing is applicable. Some employers find themselves under federal legislation in one instance and under provincial legislation in another, and I suggest that in order to remedy this particular situation some distinct and concrete steps should be taken, steps similar to those taken in 1940 or 1941 when the Unemployment Insurance Act was introduced. Maybe I have got the wrong year there. But an undertaking was made at that time to amend the British North America Act in order that the Unemployment Insurance Act should apply universally across the nation. It was, in effect, an invasion, or the giving up, if you want to look at the other side of it, of provincial jurisdiction, and that, I think, must be done in this instance to ensure the uniformity of labour legislation with regard to certification, negotiation procedures and so on, in order that we may have one set of laws throughout the country and not have confusion in the minds of management, in the minds of unions and, especially, in the minds of individual members of unions who work in different industries in different provinces at different times and find themselves governed by different sets of laws.
This may entail some adjustment in our present industrial disputes act after discussions with the provinces. If we do not succeed in having a uniform set of labour laws across the nation, then at least in so far as the federal government is concerned we need

Supply-Labour
to overhaul our legislation completely. At the present time we have a system of attempting to assist labour and management in the conduct of their affairs in so far as their negotiations are concerned, a system of conciliation boards which in some cases may operate successfully but which in many cases does not-and this applies to the provincial field more particularly, probably, because I have had a little more interest in provincial labour legislation in years past than I have had in federal legislation.
The attitudes of the various chairmen of conciliation boards is one obstacle which must be overcome. Many conciliation board chairmen still use the approach of trying to be Cyrus Ching, the second; trying to get the two parties together in order to prevent a lockout or a strike. They will confer with the unions individually, and confer individually with management and with the other members of the board in an attempt to find the solution which would be mutually acceptable and will then recommend in their awards that this should be the basis of a contract. Other conciliation board chairmen do not take that attitude at all. They sit there as if they were self-appointed lords, listen to both sides of the argument, then lock themselves up in a room and without paying much attention to the contentions of one side or the other bring forth some preconceived idea of what they think the solution is and dump it into the laps of both parties who are then no better off than they were months earlier.
I submit that the operation of the conciliation boards is outdated at the present time. It promotes delays. The hon. member for Niagara Falls mentioned a period of many months spent on negotiations between the management and railway brotherhoods, and part of that delay has been occasioned by conciliation board procedures. I am suggesting we would be moving in the right direction and laying the foundation for finding adequate solutions to differences between labour and management if we were to scrap the conciliation board procedure and have an adequately trained, tactful staff of people who would enjoy the confidence of both unions and management. Such confidence would, no doubt, need to be generated over the years. These trained conciliators would have to be intelligent and capable people, tactful and diplomatic, and they would have to enjoy the confidence of both parties so that they could meet with them both separately and collectively to help work out solutions to their problems. I am not saying that our present conciliation officers are not competent or able, but they have not been able to effect a settlement by conciliation in many

cases where strikes have taken place which in my opinion might have been avoided had we had a more sensible approach.
Further, I would suggest that any future labour legislation which is brought before this parliament, any legislation which comes under the minister's jurisdiction

and whether or not this has always been done in the past I do not know-should be referred to the committee on industrial relations, because, as we all know, it is not possible for an individual representing management or an employers' association, or for individual officers of unions, or individual citizens to come before the House of Commons or before the committee of the whole house and say: here is my thinking with respect to a particular piece of legislation. The only way in which we can offer the citizens of this nation an opportunity of expressing their views to parliament with regard to a specific piece of legislation is by referring such legislation to a standing committee so that the legislation, when it is finally developed, will reflect the attitude of the nation and, to every extent possible, of those people who will be operating the legislation and who will be affected by it. In fact, I would give this committee authority to initiate legislation, the authority to hear ideas.
In the province of British Columbia we have had for a number of years a standing committee on municipal affairs in the legislative assembly, and that committee has, in effect, authority to initiate legislation.
All that is referred to it is the general subject matter. Municipalities, unions, private corporations and individuals go to the committee every year and say, "Here are our ideas. We would like these in legislative form." Questions are asked, consultation with departmental officials occurs and legislation is initiated by that committee. I feel it would be wise to give our industrial relations committee authority to initiate legislation, to deal with legislation referred to it and recommend changes with respect to drafting. Between now and the next session I would suggest the committee on industrial relations be established as a permanent and continuing committee in order that it might sit during the period of recess and hear views and ideas and arguments and accept briefs presented to it concerning changes in our present legislation and at the next session be in a position to make some good, concrete recommendations with respect to our legislative program.
I wish to deal for a moment or two with the question of minimum wages and hours of work. That is a field which the federal government must enter with respect to employees coming under the jurisdiction of federal labour legislation. Various figures have been

suggested with respect to a minimum wage and minimum hours of work and although I have personal views on this subject I do not feel it is my duty to express them at this time although I certainly would if requested to do so. For the purposes of this context we could take the figure of $1 an hour and a 40-hour or 44-hour week. I have heard the argument expressed that there is absolutely no need for guaranteed wages with respect to employees coming under the jurisdiction of federal labour legislation, and there is no need for restrictions on hours of work or provisions for overtime. Everyone looks at the railways and says, "They are organized into unions. They do not need guaranteed wages. They are able to negotiate their own wages. They have overtime provisions. There is no need of the federal government making this a matter of legislation". I submit there is a need for this within the operations of the railways themselves.
I do not know if the condition exists today but a few years ago in British Columbia the Canadian National Railways was contracting some of the more menial jobs to outside contractors. The extra gangs, the people laying track, the spike drivers and others were not organized into unions. That work was contracted to an individual company. In fact, the possibility of organizing them appeared remote. Most of the employees on these jobs were new Canadians. There were a few from Spain but many from Italy, Portugal and other countries. They came directly from their native country to Canada, stepped off one train and on to another which took them to a location where they were immediately put to work by the contractor. They had no knowledge of the language and certainly no understanding of the wage rates or hours of work that should be in effect. They were exploited left, right and centre by the contractor. If you can imagine it in this day and age when we have laws in some provinces setting minimum wages and establishing minimum hours of work and providing for penalties for infractions of the law, these people were forced to work ten hours a day, six days a week, with no overtime provisions for 90 cents an hour. That is one group of employees that could benefit by the enactment of legislation guaranteeing a certain minimum wage and imposing a limit on the number of hours they can be required to work in a day. There are other groups, too, but I mention that one only because they worked indirectly for the railway company and were exploited by the contractors.
I notice in the estimates reference to an economics and research branch in the Department of Labour which has approximately 130 employees and involves an expenditure of
Supply-Labour
approximately $600,000. I have wondered for some time just what this branch does. I also wondered whether there is not a duplication of effort between this branch of the Department of Labour and similar branches in other government departments, especially the Department of Trade and Commerce, which deal with the economy of our country. I do not know if there is duplication but I find it strange that in the field of research into economics we do not have one branch of government to deal with the entire question of the Canadian economy for all departments of government.
My friend the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam dealt at some length with the question of unemployment and the Unemployment Insurance Act. It is not my intention to reiterate his remarks on that subject with which he dealt so effectively but I have one or two thoughts to express with respect to the Unemployment Insurance Act. I suggest it is time we began to look at the application of the act and payments of insurance benefits generally from the point of view of their being something in the nature of a guaranteed annual wage. Large industries, corporations and manufacturing units could certainly themselves bear the cost of a guaranteed annual wage covering their own employees but there are many companies in the nation that are far too small to assume the financial burden of paying a guaranteed annual wage to their employees. By establishing the policy of looking at our unemployment insurance legislation, not in terms of being a dole because a person is unemployed but in terms of a deferred payment of wages because of contributions the individual has made to the operation of an industry and/or to society we would be better off. It would spread the cost of providing additional payments while unemployed over a much broader base rather than confining it to individual industries.
Mr. Chairman, I realize that my time has nearly expired but as I have one or two additional points to make I wonder if the committee would extend to me the courtesy that was extended to the hon. member for Niagara Falls. I assure the committee I shall require just a minute or two in which to conclude my remarks.

speechtext: Is it the pleasure of the committee to agree to permit the hon. member to finish his remarks?
