speechtext: Agreed.

maintopic: EMPLOYMENT AND UNEMPLOYMENT IN CANADA FOR THE FIRST SIX MONTHS OF 1957 AND 1958
speechtext:
In conjunction with the question of changing our philosophy with respect to the Unemployment Insurance Act and looking at it in the light of attempting to

Supply-Labour
provide a guaranteed annual wage, or a deferred payment of wages during periods when people are unemployed, if you wish to classify it that way, I believe we will also have to relate to that our attitude with respect to pensions. The same administrative machinery could be used to administer the pension schemes as is used to administer unemployment insurance.
We must, I think, establish in the nation a system of allowing a person who contributes to a pension the right to transport his pension contribution with him when he moves from one employer to another. Many industries in which persons are employed for 10 or 15 years go out of business, or a curtailment is made in production. The person who has contributed to a pension plan for 10 or 15 years finds that he can no longer contribute to that pension plan because he has practically no employment, and if he goes to work somewhere else where there is no pension plan, what position is he in, if he retires 10 or 15 years hence? I suggest we should have in Canada a contributory all-inclusive portable pension plan so that a workman can move from one job to another and carry his pension contributions with him. Then, when he reaches the age of retirement he will be in receipt of a pension, in addition to the basic old age pension, adequate to look after the needs of himself and his family in his later years.
Another reason for insisting on such a system is that we find many older workers, within two or three years of reaching pensionable age, are subjected to most severe attitudes by employers in order to make them leave their jobs and thus lose their pension rights. I might add that I know of the personal experience of my own father. He was subjected to this sort of attitude by his employer in the last few years of his working life. If he had been a younger man, if he had not been so near the pensionable age, I know he would not have put up with the degrading things he was forced to put up with. I know there are many other people who have the same problem. A portable pension scheme would certainly overcome this.
With respect to the Unemployment Insurance Act itself, I hope the government will undertake to remove the discriminatory approach used with respect to contributions by and benefits to fishermen. I know there is no need to remind the minister of the promises which his party made before the last election and the election of June 10, 1957, because they are in the back of his mind and I hope he keeps them there. I hope that when the time comes to change the

Unemployment Insurance Act, which apparently is not going to be done this session, he will undertake to remember the promises which were made by the Conservative party and which I do not wish to reiterate at this time.

maintopic: EMPLOYMENT AND UNEMPLOYMENT IN CANADA FOR THE FIRST SIX MONTHS OF 1957 AND 1958
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would like to join with those who have already spoken and tell the minister that we appreciate the sincerity with which he has dealt with the many problems he has been confronted with since his appointment as Minister of Labour. We have not been able to agree with him all the time, or with the methods he and the cabinet have used to deal with those problems, but we admire his readiness and his willingness to deal with those problems.
On this vote, Mr. Chairman, I would like to deal with a particular problem. At the last session of the last parliament I introduced the following resolution:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should give consideration to the advisability of introducing legislation that would facilitate the employment in federal works, undertakings, businesses, as defined in section 2, of chapter 38 of the statutes of Canada 1956, or in any corporation set up to perform some function or duty on behalf of the government of Canada, of male or female persons over 45 years of age who, on account of their age, find it difficult to secure employment at the present time.
I know for a fact, Mr. Chairman, that hon. members from all sides of the house have encountered many instances of persons over 45 years of age who were unable to secure a job on account of their age. Some of the cases I have had to deal with were really pathetic. I have encountered during my five years as a member of parliament people over 45 years of age, able and capable of doing a good job in their particular field, but who were turned down by employers on account of their age. Thus, unable to earn their living and take care of the needs of their family, some became sick, depressed and almost a wreck. This situation creates a serious social problem in this country. This problem should be taken care of now by this government. It is our duty to put a curb on the ever-increasing tendency to discriminate against those over 45.
The problem I have just stated is an urgent one. In order to prove my assertion as to its gravity I would like to refer to the number of unemployed persons over 45 on May 24 of this year. On June 20 last, in answer to a question I had put to him on May 24, the Minister of Labour answered that in the week ended May 24, 1958 the estimated number of persons without jobs and seeking work, 45 years of age and over, was

approximately 90,000; 90,000 persons looking for jobs and almost unable to secure them on account of their age.
Compared with the social problem created by the discrimination I just mentioned, the reasons given by employers for not being too anxious to give a job to persons over 45 years old and over should not stand. All workers, no matter what their age may be, must share equally in the job opportunities. Canadians, including those over 40 and 45, should have equal opportunities in the labour market.
Some states in the United States of America, aware of the social problem I am dealing with, have enacted laws to prevent this kind of discrimination. For instance, the states of Massachusetts, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island and New York have adopted laws prohibiting discrimination against certain persons in employment on account of their age. In most of those laws the principal acts relating to age which are forbidden by law are the following:
1.	To print notices or place advertisements indicating a preference based upon age.
2.	To deny an equal opportunity to obtain employment solely because of age.
3.	To discriminate against an individual because of his age in compensation, tenure or other conditions or privileges of employment.
4.	To deny membership rights in any labour organization because of an individual's age.
5.	To deny the chance of being referred for employment because of age.
Some might feel that such a law might be difficult to enforce. If we read the first annual report of the Pennsylvania fair employment practice commission, whose job it is to see that the law against discrimination is observed in that state, we see that it has achieved good results.
Since I know the great comprehension of the Minister of Labour of problems similar to the one I have just dealt briefly with I am sure he will study carefully the laws I have mentioned in my remarks and I sincerely hope that he will see fit to bring about similar legislation in Canada at the next session.
I remember very well giving my support to the resolution presented every session by the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration while she was in opposition to the effect that this house should enact a law to promote equal pay for female employees. At every session she introduced her resolution until the government of the day decided to bring it in as a government measure. I am seeking her support today as well as the support of the Minister of Labour. Again, I hope it will be part of government legislation at the next session. As far as I am concerned, I shall continue to press the
Supply-Labour
necessity of solving this problem as long as it has not been dealt with in a satisfactory manner.

maintopic: EMPLOYMENT AND UNEMPLOYMENT IN CANADA FOR THE FIRST SIX MONTHS OF 1957 AND 1958
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have heard all the verbal bouquets tossed at the minister and I know that the finest bouquet we could present to him would be to pass his estimates as quickly as possible. I should like him to know that several members who sit on the opposition side have told me that he is the best minister of labour they can recall. I know that he gives fair and equal treatment to all members of the house no matter where they sit.
I wish to refer to two or three matters, particularly one raised by the hon. member for Skeena. He said that generally speaking we have as fine a labour movement in Canada as anywhere in the world. I believe our labour leaders are outstanding and labour has built up a fine record of greater and greater participation in our democratic form of government and our culture. Unfortunately, there are a few labour unions that do not follow the general pattern. I should like to read to the house an excerpt from a letter I received which bears out some of the implications of the remarks of the hon. member for Skeena. This man is a sailor and he writes as follows on August 8:
I wish to ask, how long must we seamen suffer extortion, intimidation, beatings-up and being D.N.Sed (do not ship), a neat way of expelling us from the union on any kind of trumped up charge or without a charge by revoking our permit, for which we pay $69, or our book. This effectively prevents us from working in the industry. To fight action for reinstatement or reimbursement through the courts requires much money, which most of us do not have to pay out to high priced lawyers such as our union hires to fight us. Why doesn't the government ban or deport Hal Banks? This man has an established criminal record; even our citizenship courts refused to grant him citizenship.
Banks has been in Canada 10 years dictating in our union. He has never run on a ballot. He is in fact a dictator who was never ever elected. He was appointed in the U.S.A.-
Then he goes on to talk about this being an intolerable situation. Actually we know that Mr. Banks was brought in by the steamship companies in order to clear out what they called the communist influence in the union of that time operating on the great lakes. This is an example of what happens when you try to tamper in the affairs of a union. In this case it seems to me that the cure was worse than the disease.
I also have a clipping from the Vancouver Province of Thursday, August 7, in which there is an article by Doug Collins telling about a union man who had to pay a $200 ' fine imposed by the union. The article reads in part as follows:
A union man paid a $200 fine last week. It was levied on him by the seafarers international union

Private Bills
because he didn't turn up for picket duty during the recent C.P.R. strike. The man, Christoph Donins of Haney, earns $238 a month. In addition to the fine, he had to pay a $28 strike levy, leaving him $10 for his first month of work this summer. The case isn't an isolated one.
The article goes on to say that when Donins protested to the strike committee about the size of the fine he was told that he was lucky, that one person who missed three watches or three times on picket duty was fined $100 and another missed one and had to pay $25. He was also told that he was lucky because if he continued in that way he would be beaten up.
Two weeks ago at a union meeting another man complained about assessments and I am informed that a Mr. Heineki wanted to know if the man complaining would like to have happen to him again what happened in 1953 when he suffered a mauling and beating up. I know that when a strike vote was taken on the west coast something over 90 per cent of the seamen supposedly voted to strike. However, the strike vote was conducted under the auspices of the union whose idea of democracy is well illustrated by what I have already said.
The largest union on the west coast is the international woodworkers of America. It is a good union, a democratic union. It has helped to raise the standards of workers in the forest industries. It is a union which is tough in bargaining but is democratically run. That union took a strike vote and found that 80 per cent of its members were in favour of a strike. They proceeded with their negotiations and the time came when a supervised strike vote was taken under the provincial labour code. In that vote the number favouring a strike dropped to 65 per cent. There were 35 per cent opposed.
That clearly indicates the fact that even when a secret vote is held by a democratic, good union the results may change when a vote is taken under government supervision. I should like to suggest to the Minister of Labour that if a supervised strike vote had been taken in the case of the S.I.U. the number favouring a strike would not have been 90 per cent or anything like it.

The house resumed, from Tuesday, August 12, consideration in committee of Bill No. S-6, respecting Trans Mountain Oil Pipe Line Company-Mr. Broome-Mr. Sevigny in the chair.
On clause 1-Subdivision of shares.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: Shall clause 1 carry?

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext:
No, Mr. Chairman. In discussing this clause I should like to point out first that there appears to be, or has appeared to be until this moment anyway, as has been expressed to me on a number of occasions, the feeling that those of us in the C.C.F. have a certain strategy in mind with respect to this particular bill, as that strategy was evidenced in dealing with this bill and with other private bills. I should just like to say that the attitude and the thoughts that have been expressed to me-and, I am sure, to other hon. members-indicate merely a tendency to jump to conclusions. I would say that one should wait until the final decision is made before attempting to say what are the ideas of any particular individual member or any particular group element in the house.
In the standing committee on this bill an amount of evidence was given and a number of opinions and ideas were expressed. I would say that certainly the greater proportion of the time of the committee was taken up by Conservative members and that many of those members-and I certainly will not do them the discourtesy of mentioning names, but the evidence is there for all to see- expressed doubt about the necessity of approving this bill. Many of them expressed fears as to what the end result would be if this bill were allowed to pass. Some of them were in outright opposition to it. Then for one

Private Bills
are participating in this company as a means of investment rather than as a means of speculation.
I might add that I have discussed this with two or three stockbrokers since that time, and I am told Trans Mountain is not an investment stock, but purely a trading and speculative stock, and that is all it will be tor some time.
I asked Mr. Renwiek about the price, and the exchanges are reported as follows:

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: If this split takes place then I assume that the price of the shares will be $12 to $15 probably on the market-or $10.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: Or $25 or $30 very shortly, especially if the situation becomes acute in the Middle East.

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: I was going to ask that question also. If this company is given permission and this bill is passed and the shares are divided five for one, the price on the market being $10 or $12, something in that neighbourhood, with no thought of issuing more of the additional shares out of the treasury and selling them on the market and some situation does develop in the Middle East, a situation similar to the Suez arises, then presumably the stocks will take another surge upwards regardless of this 10 per cent broadening and you might find yourself in the same position of trying to sell $50 or $60 shares out of the treasury. Would not your position be the same as it is now?

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext:
I think my answer to that is yes, but perhaps Mr. Taylor would like to say a word here.
Then, Mr. Taylor, who is an official of the company said:
Yes, you would be in the same position.
And the report goes on:

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext: Would you come back and ask for another stock splitting to get them down again?

maintopic: TRANS MOUNTAIN OIL PIPE LINE COMPANY
speechtext:
We would have to.
Thus, the reason was, first, that it broadened the base of ownership. Our answer to that is that it does not broaden the basis of ownership but that in effect it gives more control to the five oil companies concerned. The second reason was that it would allow the company to sell shares at a lower price than they are now quoted on the market, and the evidence throughout indicates that this is not so unless it is the intention of the company to issue those shares out of the treasury the day after this stock split takes place, if it does take place. So the answer to both these questions is in the negative.
I think we should also consider with respect to this matter all the interests which are affected by the operation of this company. We should consider what interests are affected by this request for a stock split. Some of these interests may be overlapping, but I am going to suggest that there are four. One is the interest of the company, another is the interest of shareholders, another is the interest of the general public

and the fourth is the interest of the employees. Some individuals may be concerned in more than one of these categories, but I think I can say these are the four interests affected. We must ask ourselves whether any of these interests will be advanced or whether they will be adversely affected in the over-all picture should a stock split take place.
With respect to the interests of the company, I presume it would be advanced, because the company has spent I do not know how much time down here in an attempt to get this stock split through parliament. So I would imagine it is evident that the interest of the company would be served by this stock split.
What about the interest of the shareholders? Yes, the shareholders would be well served, but only five of those shareholders. The interests that would be advanced would be those of Imperial Oil, B.A. Oil, Richfield Oil, Standard Oil of British Columbia, and Shell Oil. These shareholders would be the only ones who would receive benefit from this stock split, because their control over the company would be that much more effective than it is at the present time. When we consider that a 30 per cent interest now enables these companies to exercise control over the board of directors amounting to 66f per cent it is obvious that even a slight change in the effectiveness of that control would result in complete control over this board. The only interests that will be served will be those of the five major oil companies which have a record that is known throughout this country to be a little unsavoury.
There was absolutely no evidence given to the effect that the interest of the general public will be served. The splitting of stock five for one is not for the purpose of bringing benefit to the general public but for the purpose of broadening the base of control and reducing the price of the shares so they can sell more of them. The evidence indicates that these are not valid reasons. The arguments are not strong enough to support them. The interest of the general public will not be enhanced by the stock splitting.
With respect to the employees of the company as a part of the general public, I do not know what the position will be. Evidence was presented to the effect that the company's attitude toward its employees has been a good one and I do not wish to argue one way or the other in that respect except to say the stock splitting is not the thing that will have a beneficial effect upon the employees but the earning capacity of the company will because presumably the company will have

greater income and profits and accordingly should share these with the employees to a greater extent than at present.
I have endeavoured to make clear the reasons why we are opposed to this measure. I expressed opposition to this by voting against this clause and the preamble in the committee and I intend to express the same sort of opposition if and when it comes to a vote in this committee because, as we indicated, from all the evidence submitted it is clear that no good purpose can be served by the stock splitting. The evidence had a profound effect upon many Conservative members in the committee. I do not know whether their opinions have changed since then. It would be most enlightening if some of the hon. members who were most vociferous and who expressed the greatest amount of fear and regret in the committee would indicate to this committee why they changed their minds practically overnight.
I intend to express my opposition to the passage of this bill as I am sure will all hon. members of the C.C.F. because it will do nothing but give more effective control to five major oil companies and will do nothing beneficial for the general public.

I believe it is clear now that the rumours about our being obstructionists are far from true. We in the C.C.F. feel it is our duty and function to express our opposition to certain measures in every way possible and depending on the degree of objection of an individual member or the group to a certain measure the opposition and objection may be expressed more strenuously in some cases and on more frequent occasions than with respect to others.

Mr. Chairman, when the
committee rose I had been trying to show that the strike vote taken by S.I.U. on the west coast was not a vote in which any credence or reliance could be placed as being a true reflection of the wishes of the members. My whole point is to suggest to the minister that he might find it to advantage to survey the various legislation in use under provincial labour codes with respect to the taking of supervised strike votes.
I quite realize that this particular union is not an example of what the other labour unions are like. The overwhelming majority of Canadian unions are good unions and their leaders are honest, conscientious and hardworking men, dedicated to the job of trying to alleviate working conditions for labour and to give labour a better share of the national income but that does not minimize the fact that several thousand Canadians, for their whole working future or as long as they want to be seamen, are placed in the hands of one man-namely Mr. Banks- and that he and his men control and dictate the policies of this union. These people live under a tyranny in regard to the earning of their livelihood which can only be compared with that existing behind the iron curtain. They are assessed according to the wishes of the executive of the union, and we
Supply-Labour
know how long and how hard countries like Canada and the United States have fought for the principle of representation in regard to taxation. This right is denied to these men in respect of what is perhaps the most important field of all so far as it affects their daily life and that is the way they earn their living.
I do not have to go into detail about the background of Mr. Banks, because it is all in Hansard; it has been brought before this house on previous occasions by the present Postmaster General, the present Minister of Citizenship and Immigration and the present high commissioner at London, Mr. Drew, but I would like to quote one or two paragraphs from Hansard commencing at page 6801 for June 26, 1954, when Mr. Drew had this to say about Mr. Banks:
This man had been convicted on different occasions in the United States. One of those convictions in 1930 carried with it a sentence of fourteen years in San Quentin prison.
Later on he said the following:
But on December 5, 1947, at Richmond, California, he was charged as an ex-convict with being in possession of firearms.
And further down the page he says:
Now, Mr. Chairman, there is an old rule, which should be firmly respected, that no man is guilty unless proved guilty and there must always be a presumption of innocence. But when you see facts such as this, and when you learn that this man came to Canada and was not only convicted under the Customs Act but also twice charged and acquitted here, one begins to inquire, and surely the pattern of charges should at least be a warning to the government. One cannot disregard the fact that this man was charged on June 28, 1942, with child stealing in the United States, though there is no evidence of conviction in that case. Later he was charged with murder and acquitted.
That is what Mr. Drew had to say, and on page 6538 of Hansard for July 21, 1955, the hon. member for Kootenay West had this to say:
Quite a number of good labour people, men who have worked all their lives in the labour movement, are concerned about the damage this character is doing to the good name of labour in Canada. That is not the whole record. The government does not appear to have the whole record.
Here he was referring to the previous administration.
As a matter of fact the hon. member who spoke before me mentioned some twelve charges for carrying concealed weapons. When a man is charged twelve times for carrying concealed weapons, even though acquitted it indicates that he is a pretty tough character. He was also charged with child stealing. Beyond that we will have to leave the matter until next session,-
During last session a group of us met together and heard from certain men who had formerly been members of the seafarers international union with respect to some of the things

Supply-Labour
which went on within the union. For instance, a bookman, or trusted henchman of the union executive, would be a voting member and would have the right to lift the ticket of anybody he chose with respect to the ship in which that man was sailing or the group with which he was working. When the ticket was lifted that man no longer could be shipped; he was on what they call "D.N.S." or "Do Not Ship" and his livelihood was taken away from him until he had squared himself with the union.
It is the job of the Canadian Congress of Labour to handle its own affairs and to clean its own house, and I suggest that the labour movement in Canada, which is 99 per cent pure, should take action against unions such as this one which negate the very principle of unionism, which is that of operating a union in the best interests of the workers. It is not only a question of what we might call dragooning workers. For instance, I have a clipping from a Toronto paper which talks about teamster union boss James Hoffa having fired his outspoken critic, William Mills. Mills was secretary treasurer and business agent of the Toronto general truckers union. He was also barred for life from holding office in the union. I also know of locals which have been arbitrarily placed under trusteeship.
The former officers of the union local were fired; they were allowed to keep their union cards but have been debarred from ever holding union office, and that local no longer has the right to run its own affairs. This was done by a directive of the international president.
It is necessary that these problems be cured by labour itself, but I do suggest that they are problems on which the minister should keep his eye. Perhaps a gentle nudge now and then might help.
We would not stand for one minute for the taking away of liberties with regard, say, to elections to this house but these practices are allowed with regard to the operation of one or two labour unions, and surely the livelihood and protection of Canadians who are members of these unions is something that we as a government and as members of parliament should consider to be within our purview.

Mr. Chairman, I really want to confine myself exclusively to one topic this evening, and I am sure the minister knows already what that topic is, because I have had a good deal of correspondence about this subject with him since he became minister. I would like to say that in any correspondence I have had with the

minister or with the officials of his department or the unemployment insurance commission I have received nothing but consideration and the promptest action, and I hope the minister will not think that anything I say is intended in any way to be censorious or even really critical, except of the kind of deficiencies which I think do exist, and did exist when we were in office because of inadequacies of staff which may, of course, have been increased because of the increased volume of work which has fallen upon the insurance commission in the past year.
It is not the general work of the commission that I want particularly to talk about, but the administration of unemployment insurance for fishermen. I have in my hand a letter which has been addressed to me, and I imagine a copy was also addressed to the minister, by the general secretary of the Newfoundland federation of fishermen. It sets out a resolution unanimously adopted at the annual convention held in St. John's on April 14, 15 and 16 which embodied the views of the federation after the first year's experience in which we all knew that because this was new, and because it was complicated and because it was being applied in respect of people many of whom had very little previous experience in dealing with forms and stamps, complications would be bound to arise and cause a great many administrative headaches. I should like to read this resolution into the record. It begins:
Whereas the introduction of unemployment insurance to fishermen has been of untold benefit and assistance to our fishing population;
Perhaps even the minister would not object to my interjecting at this point that this was done by the previous administration.
-and whereas a number of problems have arisen in its first year of introduction, which was as we expected unavoidable-
These are the points which are made in the brief.
1.	The abolition of the 30 per cent cost of production. Contributions paid and benefits received on gross earnings as in all other types of employment.
To enlarge on this suggestion it might be said that where fishermen know their operating expenses these may be accepted by the employer or buyer, but we find that during the past season the majority of buyers accepted the line of least resistance and invariably deducted 30 per cent. If this cannot be abolished we suggest that a 20 per cent deduction will amply cover operating expenses.
2.	Fresh fish, salmon (fresh frozen, salted or tinned), mackerel, herring, lobsters, codoil and all other species of fish and fishery products to be treated as saltbulk or dried cod, and settlements made at the end of the fishing season and the divisor system used, as with salt cod.

I may say that personally, on the basis of such observations as I have made myself, I would very strongly endorse that view.
We would draw the attention of the commission to the position of our fishermen who can their own salmon, lobster and halibut, and who at the present time are not eligible for insurance benefits. We suggest that these be included and the divisor system used.
3.	Skippers and sharemen-We feel that stamps should be equally divided so that sharemen may qualify for benefits. At the present time the skipper has far too many stamps and the share-men insufficient. If the fish or fishery products which have been produced equally by both skipper and sharemen cannot be shared equally for insurance stamps purposes, then we suggest that the catch be divided into the number of shares plus one which would give the skipper two shares instead of half the voyage and his share of the remaining half; for example, a skipper has five sharemen in all, six men or seven shares.
I do not expect the minister to give an immediate reply to that. It is pretty technical, and it would perhaps tax me a little to give a reply myself.
4.	Clearer defining of stamp contributions and receipts for types of work other than fishing. This will have to be done in an educational manner through the press, radio and visits by unemployment insurance office officials similar to those carried out by the St. John's office during the fall of 1957.
5.	To encourage fishermen students who attend vocation or training schools during the off season period, and who had been fishing during the past year to qualify for benefits. At present students are automatically disqualified. This we consider wrong and discouraging to our ambitious young fishermen.
I am going to pause here for a moment and say that as the minister knows I feel very keenly about this question. While one can fully understand the provision in the act that anyone who on becoming unemployed goes to school is not strictly speaking unemployed, and should not therefore receive unemployment insurance, it does seem to me that in a period where there is a considerable amount of involuntary unemployment it is very discouraging indeed to these young fellows who would like to go to school to be prevented from doing so because if they do they will lose their unemployment insurance benefits. As the minister knows, I have brought several cases to his attention, and so have other hon. members from Newfoundland and, I believe, from some of the other provinces as well.
It would surely be an advantage from every point of view to have these young lads go to school when they cannot get a job. I do not think this would require an amendment to the act, but I may be wrong. I think it could be done by regulation. If the governor in council wants to stipulate that these young men should agree to accept a job if one turns up, but be allowed to go to school, I would
Supply-Lab our
not quarrel very much, though I think it would be better to give the jobs to someone who is not going to school and let them complete the term. I hope other hon. members who represent constituencies where many are engaged in the fishing industry will support me in this plea to the minister that he make this change in the regulations which could not have a very serious effect on the fund and which would in most cases increase the employability of these young people.
And then, if I may return to the document:
6.	Fishermen penalized because of employers or buyers mistakes. When the employer or buyer of stamps placed wrongly in fishermen's unemployment insurance books or places stamps of incorrect denomination, fishermen should not be disqualified because of such mistakes, but in consultation with the employer the audit office should make the necessary adjustments and the fisherman should receive the full amount of his benefits.
I am sure the minister will say that is done and I agree with him it is done frequently after a lot of labour on the part of members of parliament as well as on the part of many of the officials of his department. 7.	We strongly recommend the plan inaugurated by the St. John's office last autumn to have representatives visit various localities and meet with the fishermen and assist them with their problem, and we would suggest that this be extended to all parts of the province during the coming summer and early fall months.

We strongly urge the necessity of opening regional offices for not more than two weeks at a number of the larger settlements, especially along the northeast coast, in the strait of Belle Isle and on the Labrador. We see no necessity for the continued expense of keeping regional offices open other than for the short period during November and December when all our fishermen and many other workers are registering for unemployment insurance benefits.
Dealing with that last point particularly I would suggest a variant. I have some doubt as to whether even opening offices, except in one or two of the bigger places, would be as useful as having a number of itinerant officers who were well trained visit all the settlements, the little ones and the big ones, each officer being given a region, and really settle these problems right there on the spot where he could go to the merchant and talk to the individual and find out where the difficulties arose. It is true, of course, that my friends the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo, the hon.

I hope the minister will be able to yield to my importunities and those which I am sure he will hear from other hon. members from Newfoundland and probably from the other provinces too, but at any rate from those who represent constituencies on the east coast where the fisheries are prosecuted. I hope he will find it possible to have itinerant officers who will go around in November, December and January and visit the various settlements and settle the questions on the spot, and I really mean settle them.

Of course, there may be occasional problems of such complexity they would have to be referred to St. John's but even then I would hope they could be settled in St. John's without their having to be referred to Moncton. There are two things about the reference of these matters to Moncton that are a source of humiliation to Newfoundlanders. One is the length of time it takes and the other is the fact that the average Newfoundlander feels things should be settled in St. John's. There is a certain humiliation attached to having these matters referred to Moncton, a feeling that it is not quite right, not quite in the spirit of confederation. I am sure the minister is sympathetic with that sentimental position which, although sentimental, is also practical because reference to Moncton takes that much more time.
I do not really think I should trespass more on the time of the minister or the committee. I wish to say again how grateful I am to the minister himself and to all the officials of his department with whom I have had to deal for the courtesy and consideration they have invariably shown. But I do think it is necessary to have more staff and for the staff to be in direct contact with the customers, if I may use that term in this context.
In that connection I wonder if the minister could also give some consideration to another proposal I wish to make. I do not know how feasible this is and I would not speak about this with the same confidence with which I spoke about the previous proposal. I am quite sure I am right about the proposal concerning itinerant officers but I appreciate that there may be difficulties attached to the proposal I am about to make.
It is very worrying to those of us who represent constituencies like mine where there is no large centre or central place for people to go and where they are a long way from the nearest employment office-and I emphasize that aspect of it to the minister-people in places like Bonavista, Twillingate, Wesleyville, Fogo and other places in my district and I could go on to mention others all along the coast of Newfoundland, and in remote ridings elsewhere that they get left out to some degree in the service given to the Canadian people by the national employment office, not consciously left out but unconsciously which perhaps hurts more. I wonder if there could not be some way in which the officers having some authority could make tours and visit these places from time to time and register people and find out what their qualifications were and see to it that when jobs do open up they are not given on a first come first served basis to those

Some may think that we want to spread gloom and 57071-3-230
Supply-Labour
discouragement when we speak of this matter, but a fact is a fact. Unemployment exists at the present time and we are afraid that next winter it will be a lot worse than last winter. If we do not say anything about it, and if that comes about, we can be blamed for not telling the government that something should be done. Some may think that we are going too far. May I be permitted to cite a few remarks made by some of the ministers in 1955, when they were on this side of the house? I have in my hand remarks made by the present Prime Minister, as reported in Hansard of the session of 1955, volume II, at page 2035:
The Minister ot Labour mentioned how good conditions were six months ago. This reminded me of an old story on the prairies. A man had died in a blizzard and sympathy was given to the mourners by saying, "Just remember, six months ago yesterday was the hottest day of the year". What a hopeless picture! The government, faced for the first time with serious unemployment that has been mounting over the years, is unable to give any hope. We are unable to rouse them into placing before the people of Canada some of the picture.
At page 2036 of the same volume of the same year, the Prime Minister said:
The municipalities are loaded down with unemployment relief. The residents of our urban communities cannot bear it any longer. What is to be done about the unemployed employables? What is the attitude of the government? Well, if I understand the press of this country, almost without exception the press says that constitutional matters are today being raised as a smokescreen to relieve this government of its responsibilities. You cannot feed 550,000 hungry stomachs by promising them that if the constitution permitted it something would be done. The government adopts that attitude.
At page 2037, he said:
I repeat that we do not believe that inaction should be allowed to continue.
At page 3339 of Hansard, volume IV, of the session of 1955, the Prime Minister said:
Even on the question of unemployment the government cannot agree with itself. One department says there are 630,000 unemployed up to April, and another department says 390,000.
This is exactly the situation we had last night when we took the figures of the bureau of statistics and the figures of the unemployment insurance commission. I continue:
The minister has a revised version that does not even equal the lower figure of the two.
A little later, on page 3940, the Prime Minister said:
Certainly, the degree to which chaos is present in labour matters in this country indicates that the Department of Labour lacks direction, lacks system and lacks, not authority but direction.
These things were said by the Prime Minister of today. At the time the lady who was the official spokesman for the opposition in

Supply-Labour
labour matters-she is now Minister of Citizenship and Immigration-said, at page 1601 of Hansard for the session of 1955:
Regardless of the number of people who are out of work, regardless of whether the number is 362,000 or 569,000, the question we have to ask ourselves is whether or not hon. members and the people of Canada are going to consider that a person is merely a statistic.
Each of these 569,000 persons reported by the Department of Labour and each of those reported by the dominion bureau of statistics is a human being. Many of them have persons dependent upon them for support. It .is not only a matter of buoyancy or lack of buoyancy of the Canadian economy: it is a matter of frightened men and women with cold bodies and hungry stomachs. It is a matter of fear which grips the hearts of working people who are probably employed themselves but see their neighbours idle and who ask themselves: when is it going to happen to me? A nation is prosperous only as its people are prosperous. I think that is an accepted fact.

We cannot afford to wait. This is a time for action.

We have a country where there should be work for everybody and if we are not smart enough to organize the economy of the nation to provide work for everybody we are incompetent.

This is a problem that is national in scope. It is beyond local responsibility. What we want on the part of this government, and what we still look for, are employment measures, some constructive and some effective approach to meeting the deterioration in the economic condition and the unemployment situation in Canada today.
And on the same page there is the following:
The second problem which has been ignored by the government is the problem of unemployment. This problem has been discussed at length in this session, or I would seek to go into it at greater length today. But let me content myself, in this limited time, with making this limited observation on the subject, that the government throughout this session has observed a conspiracy of silence with regard to unemployment: and it

has carried that conspiracy of silence into the budget. It is still running away from the problem of unemployment.

As an example, we in Oshawa found last year that when the rolls showed a decrease in the number of registered unemployed of something like 600 or 700 they were the people who on April 15 were cut off supplementary benefits, but work was still not available. Mr. Chairman, we can take almost everything that was said in 1955 about the condition existing then, apply it to the present government today and the situation would be about the same, if not worse. Unemployment is a problem that we have to face. We have to face it in reality. We have to admit the fact that we are going through the summer with heavier unemployment than we had last year or the year before and that winter will soon be coming with a very grave problem falling upon our shoulders. The government will have to face up to it. The statistics furnished for the week ended June 21, 1958 show that those without jobs and seeking work numbered 320,000 compared with 162,000 in 1957 or a difference of 150,000 in those looking for work in June and not getting any unemployment benefits. These people were looking for work and were not able to get work. If things go on that way, if the numbers of unemployed increase as they have increased in the summer time then I am afraid of the winter which is coming.
Those with jobs and working less than 35 hours a week rose from 413,000 in 1957 to
501,000	in 1958, a difference of 88,000. These people are not working a full week but less than 35 hours a week and the number has increased anyway. In the case of those usually working less than 35 hours a week there is an increase of 72,000 in Canada. If we take

Mr. Chairman, I should like to join those who have congratulated the minister on the manner in which he has handled the problems of the past year. I should also like to make some suggestions as to how those problems can be handled more efficiently in the year to come. We do not want to repeat the remarks that have been made by many others and the warnings that have been given in connection with the unemployment situation. I think that these are generally understood. I am quite sure that the minister has given consideration to some of the problems. I should like to endorse the remarks made where the minister was asked to make his voice heard to see that something more would be done in that regard.
I sat this year as a member of the industrial relations committee and I have very little to say on what that committee did. But in the next year, because it is a new government and because they should have a new outlook and because labour hopes to get something better than what was developed in 1948- certainly a number of years have gone by-

we hope to see some new development take place in a federal labour code. We are in the unfortunate position federally of being able to look at some of the provinces of Canada and find that they have better labour legislation and better labour codes than has the federal government itself. Particularly because the federal government is in such a narrow and restricted labour field I think that they could quite easily set up a labour code that would be the envy of the nation and an example to the rest of the world.
In this labour code I would suggest that we set a national standard of wages, working conditions, minimum age of employment, vacations with pay; and that further we do something to assist the people across this nation in establishing equal pay for equal work. This problem has been recognized. Certainly the fair sex representatives of the government and in the cabinet have done their share to popularize this idea, as has the ladies throughout the years who have sat in the House of Commons. But still the problem exists where women who work on the same job, who have the same type of employment are not receiving equal pay. Under the federal labour code or in most of the provinces there are loopholes, particularly in the province from which I come, through which you could drive a truck. In most cases, where cases have been laid before the courts, this road through which you could drive a truck is sufficient for the able employer to duck down one of the by-ways. I therefore think the federal government could give leadership in this field. It is not a field in which it is impossible to work out a program which would be acceptable so that once women are doing the same type of work, they would receive equal pay for it.
There are other things that the labour code should protect. One of these is this. It should guarantee to labour the right to organize and to obtain union security in all public and as well as public enterprises. This matter, of course, became a problem federally in the last few months in connection with the civil service. We found that in the civil service there are several classes of employees. There are some that are civil servants and are protected by two associations which are doing a fair job in most respects. But there are classes of employees that are not covered by the civil service and therefore do not come under the jurisdiction of either one of those organizations. We have also heard of party politics being played in these particular fields. We think that the federal government should put them all into a class where they can be represented and protected and can be given the rights that workers should be entitled to

enjoy in all these matters, and this includes public as well as private enterprise.
Secondly, we should streamline conciliation procedures so as to expedite the peaceful settlement of disputes. I wish to state I am irrevocably opposed to compulsory arbitration for any reason whatsoever.
I think the Minister of Labour was very ingenious and should be complimented upon the solution he found for the recent dispute. I do not agree, and certainly none of the members of this group agree, however, that even as a last ditch resort should we accept compulsory arbitration. If it is necessary to set up an administrator in a particular field, then that administrator must be given the right to settle the problem before the problem is returned to the employer and the employees. Negotiations can be conducted on a third party basis but in no case should the employed or the employer be compelled to accept compulsory arbitration.
Thirdly, we should abolish company unions and provide effective sanctions against violations of the provisions of the act. Company unions in many cases have operated to the detriment of the employer as well as the employee and have been detrimental to the welfare of the national economy as well as to the companies concerned. When company unions grow and become federations they in all cases work out to the detriment of the people who set them up in the first place, and we feel they should be outlawed.
These are only some of the things which must be included in a federal labour code, and I am quite sure the minister has been giving these matters consideration and that probably in the next year or two we will develop a new national labour code which will be as good as, if not better than any of the codes in the provinces across the country.
I would like to mention a matter which was discussed in committee and that is the question of international unions which has become a problem in the last few years. They have been built up for various reasons and I think the time has come to say something good and something bad on this aspect of the labour situation. I belonged for a number of years to the steelworkers' union of America, which is an international union, and I was later employed by the international woodworkers of America union. I have had a considerable amount to do with both of these unions and I believe they are a credit to unionism and to the people of Canada. In a number of cases-and this is particularly true of the international woodworkers' union of America -the Canadian membership outnumbers and outranks the United States union membership but they have made no effort to change
Supply-Labour
the structure in order to create a national union, which they could have done quite easily by a vote at any of their conventions. The Canadian union had a majority and could have seceded from the union and become a national union had they wished to do so, but there are many advantages to belonging to an international union.
The reason why these unions grew was because the companies involved also became international companies. I have dealt with companies which are controlled by and are, in many cases, only subsidiaries of United States companies, and in many cases these United States companies have not given consideration to the Canadian economy and the Canadian way of life, but only in a very few cases have they set up their subsidiary companies in such a way that the policies were different in Canada from those in the United States. The unions have found, when dealing with such companies as Johns-Mansville that the United States company has set up their negotiators to consider the Canadian situation from the United States point of view, and the unions would be in a very bad position if they did not have some official who could be called in and who could handle the situation as it related to the United States situation.
I believe, however, there are very few of these unions which have not turned over the majority of control to their local Canadian union, and I have personally sat on wage policy committees with respect to the steelworkers of America. I have also sat on a Canadian wage policy committee and I can assure the house that the decision of such a conference was not similar in any way to those in the United States. We were not concerned with the situation which had developed in the United States wage policy conferences, but were considering the conditions which existed in this country and which were not always similar to those in the states. Our conditions are usually much poorer from an economic point of view than those across the border, and I think I can say with some authority that the financial set-up of the union has been criticized because in many cases money flows from Canada to the United States. It is true that the international treasury is often in the United States, but this money is a book balance for the purpose of transferring dues to that country. The money is deposited in almost every case in Canadian banks and does not go to the United States.
Speaking for the unions to which I belonged, and I was active president for a number of years of a mining union, the money which was brought into Canada to

Supply-Labour
assist us with respect to very serious problems in the gold mining industry in 1953 will not be equalled in the next hundred years by the amount of money collected in dues from Canadian miners in that area. This United States money was sent for our assistance and does not take into consideration the money spent helping us to organize and to carry on the business of that union. So I think something should be said for these international unions, and I would also point out that their accounting systems in most cases, though very large and adaptable, do prevent problems which have developed in all unions with which I have had anything to do.
Mention has been made of one international union which is a bad one, but I would suggest that you do not just find unions which are bad and union officials who are bad without also finding bad employers. You do not find them separately. One particular case which affects the Canadian people is with respect to a certain gentleman who was brought to Canada to break a communist-dominated union. That might be good or it might be bad, but it is certainly no credit to the Canadian people that they should need co-operation from outside in order to do the job. The gentleman who was brought in had a record of which no labour man would be proud. I suggest that he came in in this instance with the co-operation of the federal government, which acted in its roundabout role as employer in the shipping industry in connection with a matter of which we have disposed. The government assisted in bringing him into Canada and allowing him to operate under the conditions necessary to perpetuate bad unions and bad union representation. If the representative of the union has no power to fire the men in his employ, to intimidate them or to keep them in subservience, then he cannot remain in that position because they will vote him out. But in this particular case the government assisted in keeping that particular gentleman in his position, and if hon. members check the records of the investigations in the United States with respect to the teamsters union they will find that in all cases where the union became corrupt there was also a great deal of corruption on the part of employers.
Check the record and you will find no union can fire employees. They have not that right. They always obtain this treatment by working out a dead with the employers. Where employers and unions are bad you will find these corrupt practices and I suggest that they are so limited in Canada and happen so rarely that they make headlines when they do. There are now over a million

union members in this country and there are very few of them who are bad.
There is another problem which the minister could examine if he saw fit, and that is the matter of choosing a union. The minister was involved in the pipe line industry and in the affairs of the Northern Ontario Pipe Line Crown Corporation and in this particular case one of the things that should never happen in unionism happened. There were a number of companies given contracts and these companies had no employees. They went out and negotiated yellow dog contracts with unions who had no membership in that area and when the employees were hired in this case they were told they were going to pay dues to a particular union and that they would not have any choice in the matter. This problem has become acute because these employees on that line are still not represented. I have a letter from a man who paid $90 in dues in nine weeks and who wrote me to find out what unions he belonged to. These conditions exist because of these yellow dog contracts being signed and the government must bear some responsibility because this concerns a crown corporation.
Also, it is understood that at the end of the 11 or 12 months in a normal contract year the employee has the right to decide collectively whether or not he wants the same union to represent him in the coming year. In cases where the employer and the bargaining agent get together and make a deal they take away that right from the worker, because if there has been a contract signed in that period of time the two month period is no longer applicable because the contract is binding on both parties. This is done without holding a membership meeting; in some cases without there being any employee from that union present. The contracts are signed, and the members are away for another ride for another year with the same thing happening again.
The people who say that the unions have strayed from the job they are supposed to do had better take a look at the employer because he also had to do his share and they will find that the blame does not rest alone on either side. This is a field in which the minister could become involved for the benefit of all Canadian workers. There must be some policing of the gross negligence that sometimes takes place, and I think that labour itself would be very happy to have him put in an administrator when these conditions exist and hope he can straighten them out and put them back on the straight and narrow. In all cases when the employees know what the conditions are they are quite willing to take a stand and do something

about them themselves. I think this is a field that the government has already entered because of the conditions they have encountered on the pipe line, and I am sure they must exist in many other fields.
Another problem which has been mentioned in the committee and which I should like to comment on now is the situation where the courts of Ontario decided that the federal government was going to be involved in certification and in the handling of the problem of the uranium workers. I have in my riding hundreds and hundreds of people who are working in the uranium fields in Blind River and the Elliott lake area. They are mostly either Timmins or Kirkland Lake people who have gone there because of the wage structure and they are having a terrific problem in Blind River. This falls under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Labour. The minister was handling these certifications, but I understand they were turned back to the provincial government by the Ontario courts. The government of Ontario has failed for years and years to do very much for the safety of the mining people working in the mines. The rate of accidents in the mines is very heavy. The silicosis problem, which they could have ended many years ago with laws which would have ventilated the mines rather than putting aluminum dust into people's lungs has not been dealt with. In Blind River they are killing people off every day because they have not the time to implement the proper safety regulations.
I suggest that the minister should take these mines back under his jurisdiction and put in honest inspectors, inspectors who do not go to the mine and hang up their clothes and say to themselves: now that is not going to give the company very much notice. But the mining companies know full well that the inspector cannot go anywhere else until he has picked up his clothes, and that the inspection is going to happen there. It is the same thing as members of the House of Commons committee found when they walked over to the printing bureau. When they found that the Department of Public Works had supplied all the fans in town-

It was known when the inspector brought his clothes on Friday, because he left them over Saturday and Sunday and that the inspection usually came on Monday, by which time things were usually in fairly good shape. If these inspections came under the minister, conditions would not be the same in these uranium mines.
I should be happy if the gold mines were placed under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Labour, because if such action is justified in the case of the uranium mines the same justification applies in the case of the gold mines inasmuch as the government buys the product and pays a subsidy with regard to its production. In these respects it is similar in nature to the uranium product. I should like to see something constructive done to bring this under the federal code, particularly when I am sure the minister is going to bring it up to the standard of the best province in Canada and probably a little higher. Certainly the people in the industry would appreciate it.
Another problem is the matter of a national pension plan. Certainly, in the field of mining, a national pension plan is a problem which is before the workers and their bargaining agents all the time. Such workers have a tendency to fluctuate from mine to mine and from area to area and that is a good thing. It is the only thing which made it possible for us to develop our resources in the mining field. But I think consideration should now be given to putting in a national pension plan for them. The pension would be supplementary to the basic national pension of $75. It would be contributory. It should be compulsory for a miner working today to pay a percentage of his wages to a pension plan and the employer should be compelled to pay an equal or a greater amount to the plan.
This would be administered by the government and be transferrable from mine to mine, from industry to industry and from field to field. A miner who worked a number of years in the gold mines and then transferred to the nickel mines could carry his pension with him and when he decided to go to Windsor and work in the automobile industry his pension would be transferred. At the end of 20 or 25 years during which he would have worked in various industries in different parts of the country he would have a decent

Supply-Labour
pension and could retire and live out his last days without asking for a handout. He would have contributed to the pension throughout his lifetime and it would bear a relationship to the wage he had earned throughout that working period.
I urge the minister to give consideration to this type of pension plan. The minister knows full well that most miners have a short working life and live in poverty for a number of years before they die. The wages in the mines have not been sufficient to permit them to buy government annuities implemented by the Department of Labour in years gone by for a similar reason. I feel confident the minister will take action in the field of pensions and thus benefit many people.
I have only one other matter to raise this evening and that is the question of statistics. The Department of Labour has a large research and statistical branch and the work it does is also done by similar branches in other departments of government. This indicates that we should either expand this branch in the Department of Labour and the Department of Trade and Commerce or else expand the work of the bureau of statistics.
Frankly, I am inclined to believe that the bulletin produced by the Department of Labour is superior to that produced by the dominion bureau of statistics because it contains more accurate, up to date and reliable figures. Perhaps it would be a good idea to dispose of the dominion bureau of statistics and enlarge this branch. We are in no position to finance this type of research work in a number of government departments and duplication could be avoided. The material compiled by the dominion bureau of statistics is not always completely accurate because unions and private firms do not like to make full disclosure of their statistics. I have sought on a number of occasions to use this information during negotiations but I have discovered there are other sources which provide more up to date information concerning wages in plants and industries. Some consideration must be given either to expanding or decreasing the work of the dominion bureau of statistics.
With respect to the duplication of effort we find that the results of the two bodies are not always the same. The figures released by the statistical branch of the Department of Labour sometimes bear little or no relationship or similarity to the figures released by the dominion bureau of statistics. I believe we should consider either increasing the work of this branch or amalgamating it with the dominion bureau of statistics.

Mr. Chairman, although there are those who may not attach much importance to the department whose estimates we are being asked to vote, I consider it to be one of the most important government departments, considering that I represent a riding with a large labour population.
In my riding, where 75 to 90 per cent of the constituents are workers, the unemployment problem has been very acute for the past few months. Every week-end I am visited by scores of people who ask me to help them. They include people who are no longer drawing unemployment insurance benefits, yet who have three, four or five children and are without any means. Accordingly their only hope is to go to the St. Vincent de Paul society in their parish, but these charitable organizations ran out of funds last winter, leaving these poor souls with no choice but to walk the streets, cap in hand. Not a single section of the department does anything to help them.
It is all very well to give us these statistics, but they are inaccurate inasmuch as they ignore those who cannot draw benefits and those who are not registered in the unemployment insurance offices. There are all too many people who, while no longer drawing their benefits, are left out of government statistics. The latest statistics available, dated June 21st, show 320,000 persons seeking employment. This is acknowledged to be a record since the war, for the highest number so far was in 1954, I think, when there were 186,000. This makes today's figure a record for unemployment in Canada.
Speaking only of Montreal, there were as of June 19, 1958, 61,000 registered unemployed, whereas on June 20, 1957, there were only 29,900, which means that there are now twice as many. Last week, when I went to an unemployment insurance office with some citizens who thought they had a good chance to obtain something, a member of the staff of that office told me that this year they had paid out just double the amount of last year. It can therefore be said that in the city of Montreal, the government is now paying twice as much in benefits as last year, and that the number of unemployed has doubled, not counting those who are not registered.
You will remember that, during the conference called last July, federal and provincial ministers of labour studied the problem of seasonal unemployment. After the conference, the minister of labour of British Columbia complained that neither his colleagues nor himself had an opportunity to make any

suggestions in this matter. Moreover, it seems that no definite suggestion was made by the federal government on that occasion. It is also to be noted that no report to the house was made on the matter by the Minister of Labour. We can therefore blame the government for not having announced any project which might have been of assistance to those who are suffering from seasonal unemployment, or those who will suffer from it next winter, for their number will certainly be much greater.
According to the last statistics I just mentioned, it is obvious that there were 320,000 unemployed in Canada in the month of June, twice as many as last year. In spite of this serious situation, the government does not want to extend the period of unemployment insurance benefits during the summer months, and still considers that unemployment as seasonal. It is obvious that it is more than a seasonal situation and that the government should assume that responsibility for the whole year.
In that connection, Mr. Chairman, allow me to suggest to the Minister of Labour, in order that he may deal with the unemployment situation in Canada and particularly in Montreal, that a standard should be set so that as soon as unemployment exceeds a certain figure, the government may act at once. In my opinion, the Department of Labour should use the number of unemployed in 1957 as a basis for future years. It is known that, in 1957, there were from 160,000 to 170,000 unemployed and that, at the present time, there are about 320,000, or about twice as many. It means therefore that there is acute unemployment and that our Canadian citizens are in need. It is the responsibility of the government to help the unemployed as it must feel responsible for it.
This government seems to enjoy setting records. After a record deficit from the Minister of Finance, we are today witnessing a record number of unemployed, that is 320,000.
I repeat that, in my opinion, the government should, when a crisis is upon it, as it is this year, when all the funds provided are expended, assume year round responsibility for the unemployed and help them meet the needs of their families.
I suggest that the government should intervene to help the unemployed when the level of unemployment reaches a certain high mark, let us say that of 1957. The present unemployment situation is all the more serious because people who are unemployed at this moment will remain unemployed next winter. How can they obtain sufficient stamps to qualify for 57071-3-231
Supply-Labour
unemployment insurance next winter if they cannot work during the summer? As everyone knows, any worker who suddenly loses his job and who resumes work later, must accumulate a credit of 30 weeks of work to be entitled to his meagre pittance in the form of unemployment insurance. What will the present unemployed do now that they are drawing no benefits, and what will people do next winter who are about to cease getting their benefits? Can you imagine the untold number of unemployed and the misery that will prevail throughout the country next winter? I am not wishing that it will be so, Mr. Chairman, but I fear that next fall and next winter will be seasons of hardship for our Canadian workers. How does the government intend to ensure that these unemployed will not be without work indefinitely?
Since the Conservative government has been in power it has done nothing to help the Montreal unemployed to find jobs.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a few words in English to confirm what I said in French and so that the minister may understand better what I just said in French. I am of the opinion that the unemployment problem should be handled on a different basis. In June, 1957 there were some 160,000 people unemployed in Canada. In June 1958 there were 320,000 people out of work in Canada. The government and the Minister of Labour should inaugurate some system by which we could take care of the unemployed.
We do not like to recall the depression years when whole families were on the dole. In many instances their only food was what they received on the bread line. Workers experienced a period of abject poverty. Life was not worth living. Parents and children were practically starving and dying of hunger and cold. Everybody remembers the 1930's in Montreal. I know something about it. I was living in the city of Montreal. Montreal is still paying off the debts that it incurred to support the out-of-work people in Montreal at that time.
I have a press clipping from the Vancouver Sun of July 25, 1958, and I should like to read the following extract:
Provincial labour minister Lyle Wicks' diagnosis of Ottawa's attitude to unemployment confirms what the Sun has several times suggested.
The Diefenbaker government is determined to ignore what properly ought to be called "recessional unemployment".
At the recent municipal-provincial conference on the jobless problem, Mr. Wicks complains, Ottawa tried to restrict discussion to seasonal unemployment. It would limit discussion to what may be expected this winter.
At that, Ottawa has a right to be concerned about the coming winter. As Alderman Halford Wilson said, unemployment is bad enough now and likely to be worse in the winter if preventive steps are not taken. The same day he said it, the local unemployment insurance office warned that "no significant improvement can be expected in the near future."
How true this could be is shown in official figures this week disclosing 320,000 Canadians out of work in mid-June. This is a decline of 46,000 from May but double the figure of a year previous.
As to the suggestion I made a few minutes ago, I have a press clipping from the Toronto Star dated July 14, from which I should like to read the following extract:
There are two ways the federal government can provide for those who will need help. It can change the Unemployment Insurance Act at this session

of parliament, lower the requirement that six months steady work must take place between first and second claims for insurance. Or, if it feels that this would remove the insurance principle from the act, it can make special provision for those unemployed who will not qualify for aid. Either way, the government must be prepared to take care of men and women out of work through no fault of their own.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I ask that the government and the Minister of Labour pay special attention to the unemployed people in Canada. I deplore unemployment myself because I represent a constituency consisting almost wholly of labouring people. I know what the unemployed suffer. I again ask that the government and the Minister of Labour enact some measure, if at all possible, so that in bad years like 1958 the unemployed people will be taken care of by the government 12 months in the year, if that is necessary. This will help the people of Canada, and we are here to protect them as far as we possibly can. I would like to see more people working next winter.
