speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a few words on this subject. First, I should like to congratulate the Minister of Labour and the government for the action they took last year with regard to unemployment by increasing the amount of weekly benefits available to persons covered by unemployment insurance. I think this is clear proof that the government is discharging its responsibility and should a situation similar to that of last winter arise again I am confident that the government will do its best to come to the help of the unemployed. Something should be done, said the hon. members for Hull and St. Ann, but apparently they are unaware that something has already been done. A lot of things have been done by the government and if no action had been taken when the government took office we would have a much worse situation than last year. As proof of this one only has to look at what has happened across the border since then. However, it is most encouraging to note that the United States economy is on the recovery road and the results should be felt in Canada later this fall and throughout next year. One only has to look at today's newspapers to get an idea of the optimistic opinion now prevailing in the United States. The impact of their recovery will be felt in Canada all the more now that the new Progressive Conservative government has repaired our own economy in all sectors. It is reported in today's newspapers that the automobile industry is now staging a spectacular recovery across the border and United States businessmen are confident that 1959 will be a record year. For all these reasons

I believe that the attitude of the Minister of Finance when he presented his budget will be proved to be right and that we may well find that he was not optimistic enough with regard to the year 1958.
What has been done by the government speaks for itself. The record is there and the facts are known throughout the country. Of course, there are still a few clouds in the economic sky but the situation has improved steadily since the government took office. In all sectors of the economy, including employment prospects, official figures across the country clearly indicate that that is so. For the purpose of having it on record I should like to read some extracts from an article that appears in a paper published in my region. I am pretty sure that the hon. member for Hull can see the headline. It is headed, "Employment Prospects Looking Good; Improvement Says Local Commission." The article appeared in the Val d'Or Star of August 13 and reads in part as follows:
Statistics issued for the months of July and August by the commission manager, Mr. M. Decarie, revealed Val d'Or and immediate district as now being placed in one of the best employment areas of the country. In some respects, employment conditions are ahead of those existing a year ago. Despite the fact that businessmen in town describe this summer as "poor" in connection with tourism, the commission states that more jobless have been taken on in this field than there were during the same period last year.
In his report Mr. Decarie says that mine employment has shown a marked improvement in activities in all spheres. This, he comments, has been the best month for mine workers since last year. Operations in the bush are remaining steady, and so far there has been no suspension of work as there was last year.
Construction too has shown a considerable upturn over the past eight weeks, and again employment prospects here are way ahead of a year ago. More building projects over a wide area of northwestern Quebec have accounted for the upsurge in employment among construction workers. In some areas, the Star learned this week, it is becoming difficult to obtain skilled building workers.
Commerce and transport industries were also well to the fore during July and August, and a steady improvement was recorded in these two employment categories.
This shows, Mr. Chairman, that the public works program and the actions that have been taken, by the government are being felt throughout the country because my area is a remote one and we are feeling the improvement right now. That is not all that is said in this article. I should like to read the last paragraph, which is as follows:
Although many cities and towns throughout the country are anticipating the coming winter with grave apprehension in employment prospects, commission officials in Val d'Or are quietly optimistic that we shall not reach the depressing unemployment figures reached here last spring.

Mr. Chairman, there is one matter which I should like to bring to the minister's attention and I believe this is the only item on which it can be raised. However, before I deal with it I should like to associate myself with the pleas made this afternoon by the hon. member for Cartier and the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam for the establishment of institutions to train teachers as vocational training instructors. I should also like to associate myself with the request made by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate.
The matter which I wish to bring to the minister's attention has to do with the Merchant Seamen Compensation Act which 1 believe is administered by the Department of Labour. Perhaps I can save time and illustrate my point better by describing an actual case. One of my constituents lost his life at sea and left behind a wife and several children. The wife and children received an allowance under the Merchant Seamen Compensation Act. Susequently the mother died leaving the children as orphans.

Subsequently the mother died leaving the children alone in the world. These children were taken into the home of their married sister who acted as a foster mother and after a time the allowance under the Merchant Seamen Compensation Act was restored but because of the wording of this act it was impossible for the foster mother to receive the regular allowance. The reason for that was that the Merchant Seamen Compensation Act stipulates that in order to qualify for an allowance the foster mother must move into the house where the children originally lived. To me that seems to be a rather senseless requirement.
If you take into consideration the situation of a merchant seaman you will find that he is an ordinary person. He is not likely to have a very big bank account and the mother

Supply-Labour
who is obliged to exist on charity and allowances is going to find it difficult to keep that house in proper repair. In this case the children were taken out of the house in which they lived and were moved into the sister's house in the same community, only a few yards away from where they originally lived.
Surely we in this parliament with that legislation should be concerned about the welfare of the children and not about keeping establishments open. In this case the children have moved into a better home than they had previously. Yet their foster mother is deprived of the allowance because of the wording of the Merchant Seamen Compensation Act. I think that fact indicates that this legislation needs to be overhauled, and I would ask the minister to give the matter serious consideration.

Representing as I do a riding which is mostly made up of members of the labouring forces, I think there is no doubt that I am as concerned as is any other member about the unemployment situation and as anxious to take part in this debate on the estimates of the Minister of Labour. Since we are dealing with the estimates I should like to take advantage of the opportunity to ask two questions of the minister in connection with the compilation of unemployment figures. From month to month we receive one set of figures compiled by the dominion bureau of statistics and another one compiled by the unemployment insurance commission. When the minister was sitting on this side of the house I well remember how dissatisfied he was with these two sets of figures. Since we have today more unemployment than we had a year ago, I submit that we should try to improve the system of compilation that we have. With the various offices of the national employment service covering almost every area of this country, I do not see why a more accurate system of compilation with regard to unemployed persons cannot be established. The more accurate such a system is, the easier it would be to bring relief to a specific area where unemployment is more serious than it is in another one.
This brings me, Mr. Chairman, to a question I should like the minister to answer. The Minister of Labour has reiterated many times that the reason why the figures of the national employment service were set aside was that the monthly report included a number of persons who already have a job and are applying for another one. If this is the only reason-and the minister has never

given another one-for not using these figures, I should like now to quote the latest report issued by the national unemployment service. On the bottom of this report we read that the count excludes registrations from persons known to have a job and applying for another one. It therefore seems that we are entitled now to an explanation by the minister on this point, because the reason he has given many times in this house is contradicted by the latest report we have received from the national employment service.
I know that the dominion bureau of statistics does not fall under the jurisdiction of the Department of Labour but since the minister is using these figures I should like to have from him some explanation as to how these compilations are made. I hope that the minister in his remarks before the item is voted upon, will care to give us some comment on those two particular points that I have raised.
